A developer has no command or snippet on the home page.

ref:vercel.com.notes: Excellent type and restraint (the tight grotesk headline, the generous whitespace), but 'Agentic Infrastructure' with a triangle says little to a newcomer in ten seconds, and the page has almost no figures besides a customer stat. v1.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Make the pencil digits work, in every cell, desktop-light-00 and desktop-dark-top. The tails after the three ink places are set at about 8 px in low-contrast grey, so they can't be read. They have no right padding, so the long ones run into the column rule: row 02 c6i '3.883 593 521 982 312 7', row 06 every column ('0.858 435 309 448 242 2'), row 02 m5. Their grouping is irregular too: groups of three, then a stray single digit, and a different count per cell. Fix it at the source. Give each column a fixed tail width sized to the longest tail it holds, with padding before the rule. Set the tail in tabular figures one size step below the ink (not three) and at a contrast that passes, and group from the decimal point in threes so the stray digit always falls in the same place. The idea of exact digits with three places in ink is the best thing on the page, and at the moment it costs legibility.
2. Show which way is better, and help the eye compare across a row. GB/s (higher is better) sits next to ns, ms and µs (lower is better), and nothing says which way to read. Put a small 'higher is better' or 'lower is better' mark beside each unit (UNIT column, desktop-light-00; the unit at the right of each benchmark title on phone). Then add one quiet comparison cue per row: the best cell in ink-bold or underlined, or a hairline bar under each figure scaled to the row. Today a reader has to parse 70 long numbers to see that c8a wins memory and that m5 is 7× slower on syscall.
3. Show the spread and the count behind each figure. The Method keeps p5, p50 and p95, but the ledger shows only p50 and never how many Runs stand behind it. Under each median, add a one-line pencil row such as 'p5 12.49 · p95 12.51 · n 34'. Or put a single small range tick in the cell. This is what makes rows 10–14 meaningful: whether 131.284 against 131.094 is a difference or noise.
4. Say in the table itself when a row measures the volume or the service rather than the machine. Row 10 (all 131.1 MB/s, the gp3 baseline of 125 MiB/s), row 12 (all 333.3 µs, i.e. the 3,000 IOPS gp3 baseline), row 13 and row 14 are flat across machines. A newcomer will conclude that the machines are equal, or that the benchmark is broken. Add a short note in the NOTE column: 'Capped by the gp3 volume's 3,000 IOPS baseline; same on every machine.' Also fix row 12's description, 'How many direct reads … completes', when the figure is a time per completed read in µs. Either state it as time per read or also give the reads per second.
5. Phone, phone-light-04: the Machines table is clipped at the right edge. The processor names are cut ('Gran', '9R', '837') and the NETWORK and USD AN HOUR columns can't be seen at all, so on a phone the prices never appear. There is no scroll cue either. Make it a stacked card per machine, or two lines per row: type, vCPU and memory, then processor and price. On phone, also put each machine's price once in the per-benchmark tables, or in a sticky machine key, since the desktop header's prices are lost there.
6. Make the figures look like links if they are links. The intro says 'Each figure links to its Series' file', but no figure looks clickable in any screenshot. Give them a hover or underline treatment, or a small ↗ on the row. Showing a path to the evidence is the trust claim, so it should be visible.
7. Agents section (desktop-light-01, right half). The three curl commands and the URL list repeat the same three addresses. Keep the curl blocks, fold the schema URLs into a compact list, and add a short excerpt of a real Series response so a developer sees the shape (percentiles, n, method, evidence links) without fetching. Consider moving a one-line 'curl api.ledgermath.com/v1/index.json [COPY]' into the header meta block, which today has only a link. The section sits about two screens down.
8. Header meta (desktop-light-00, top right): the nanosecond timestamp '17:07:23.182448102 UTC' is honest but noisy where it appears first. Lead with something a person can read, such as 'Newest Run 2026-11-19 17:07 UTC, 52 min ago', and keep the full stamp in pencil or in 'How a figure is kept'. The phone version (phone-light-00) is a long block of text with no figure above the fold except the start of row 01; this would tighten it.

KEEP
The point of view: a 'book of record', ink and pencil, roman-numeral sections, double rules, Source Serif with Plex Mono for machine names. It is distinctive and carried through consistently, and nothing like a SaaS template. Also keep the one-sentence purpose paragraph at the top, the price in each machine column header, the cheapest-first column order, the NOTE column's definition of each repetition, the 'How a figure is kept' glossary with the kept, counted and failed counts, AWS's own price wording quoted, and the 70-of-187 selection rule stated under the table. The phone ledger, a small table per benchmark, is a real redesign, not a squeezed desktop. Dark mode keeps the character and reads well.

READS AS FALSE OR MISLEADING
Nothing looks invented, but four things will make a careful reader stop. (a) 'RUNS AT 04:10 · 10:10 · 16:10 · 22:10 UTC' next to a newest Run at 17:07:23 and an oldest at 23:36:41: say that a Run finishes some time after its boot, or the schedule looks wrong. (b) 'FAILED, KEPT 0' out of 6,335 looks too clean without context. If it is true, the italic definition beneath it helps; consider linking to where a failure would be shown. (c) The 'how many' wording in row 12 against a figure in µs (see 4). (d) The flat disk and S3 rows shown without explanation can read as a defect in the measurement.

v2.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Put the spread on the page, not behind hover. DATA says 'hover for p5 and p95' (desktop-light-00, the paragraph above the table). Hover doesn't exist on a phone, doesn't show in a screenshot, and is invisible to a reader skimming. For a project whose whole case is exact, honest numbers, showing p50 alone hides the one thing that tells you whether two machines really differ (e.g. syscall 93.241… vs 93.242… on i4i and c6i, or GET-from-S3 22.59 vs 22.93). Add a small p5–p95 line or a faint range tick under each figure, at the same weight as the n= line.
2. Phone rows drop the provenance. On phone-light-01 to -03 each benchmark shows machine plus figure only: the n= count and the Series link (the hash) that desktop prints under every figure are gone. STATUS still promises 'linked from each figure'. Put n (and the range from change 1) on phone as a third, dim column or a second line. It costs little height and keeps the page's main promise on every screen size.
3. Say what the disk rows actually measure. 'Read a file sequentially' is 131.0–131.3 MB/s on all five machines, and 'Random 4 KiB, 64 in flight' is 333.3 µs everywhere (desktop-light-01, the DISK group). Those numbers are the gp3 volume's provisioned limits (125 MiB/s, 3,000 IOPS), not anything about the machines. An agent estimating a cost from this page will wrongly read them as machine properties. Add a one-line note on each affected row (or on the DISK heading) saying the figure is the volume's cap. Treating the cause beats leaving five identical numbers to explain themselves.
4. Help comparison across a row. Each row shows five 17-digit strings and no direction. Add 'higher is better' or 'lower is better' next to the unit (the rust GB/s and µs at the left), and mark the best figure in each row with a subtle mark (weight or an underline, not a colour flood). Comparing machines is the main job of this table, and today the reader has to work out direction from the unit.
5. Get a figure above the fold. On desktop-light-00 the first 900 px end at the machine header row, so a newcomer sees no measured number on the first screen. Shorten the paragraph under SYNOPSIS (it repeats what FILES says), or pull the first benchmark group up beside SYNOPSIS, so that at least one row of real figures shows on the first screen. The page's claim is 'measured figures'; show one immediately.
6. Fix the copy that contradicts the units. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' says 'How many direct reads … completes' but the unit is µs per read. 'Sort 1 MiB' and the memory rows say 'How fast' over a time unit. 'Lock and unlock a mutex' repeats '(10,000 critical sections)', and its µs-per-10,000 forces mental division; consider saying ns per lock/unlock pair, or saying so plainly. In MACHINES the network column mixes 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit'; normalise it, or label it as AWS's own wording.
7. Stronger landmarks in the long table. The group headings ('## MEMORY', '## COMPUTE' …) are small rust caps, about the same size as the row text. The three description lines per row (description, italic 'one repetition', italic 'setting') are small, grey and long, so on desktop the 14 rows blur together. Give the groups more space and weight, and consider putting 'one repetition / setting' on a single line in a lighter, collapsible register. The 'p50' label sits alone at the left of the machine-header row; move it to head the unit column, where it means something.
8. The series hash under each figure (a0faf4326dd7, etc.) reads as noise to a person. Either make the figure itself the link and drop the hash, or prefix it with something readable ('series ↗', 'evidence'), so its purpose is clear without reading the DATA intro.

STRONG — KEEP
- The man-page concept (LEDGERMATH(5), NAME/SYNOPSIS/DESCRIPTION/EXIT STATUS/FILES/SEE ALSO) suits a project that publishes a file format for developers and agents, and it is carried through with real discipline, header to footer. It is distinctive and not a template.
- STATUS: newest and oldest Run to the nanosecond, kept/counted/failed, schedule, zone, price copy time. This is the best freshness-and-provenance block of any page in the comparison set.
- SYNOPSIS: three real curl lines with comments and copy buttons, plus FILES and schemas in SEE ALSO. The way in for an agent is obvious within seconds.
- Exact figures that are decimal-aligned, with the first four significant digits bright and the rest dim. This keeps the no-rounding promise while staying scannable. The per-row 'one repetition' and 'setting' definitions are excellent.
- METHODS in plain text with the R type 7 formula and the 'counted' rule, and EXIT STATUS '0 Runs failed of 6,335': trust you can audit.
- The phone version is designed, not squeezed. Per-benchmark machine lists with aligned decimals, and machine cards in place of the wide table.
- Dark mode: the amber accent on near-black is well judged, and the hierarchy holds.

READS AS FALSE OR MISLEADING
- On phone, 'hover for p5 and p95' and 'linked from each figure' promise things the phone layout doesn't visibly give.
- The identical disk figures, with no note, invite the false reading that all five machines have the same storage performance (see change 3). i4i.2xlarge even lists a local 1875 GB NVMe in MACHINES, which makes the 131 MB/s look like that machine's disk speed when it is the EBS root volume's.
- 'How many … completes' over a µs unit (the Random 4 KiB row) states the wrong kind of quantity.

v3.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first
1. Get figures onto the first screen. On desktop-light-00 the top 900 px holds the title, timestamps, the abstract and the Data availability box; the first number (Table 1) starts around y=1790, after an Introduction that mostly repeats the abstract. Fold the Introduction's three points (i-iii) into the abstract or a short line under it, move Methods (section 4) below Access (section 5), and start Table 1 directly under the abstract/Data availability block. A benchmark home page should show a benchmark above the fold; vantage and ClickBench show data straight away.
2. Make Table 1 a matrix you can scan in one view. Right now each of the 14 rows carries a two-line description, so the 14x5 table runs to about 1.3 desktop screens and you can't compare one machine across benchmarks without scrolling. Drop the descriptions to one short line in smaller type (or move them into the Figure 1 captions, where they already partly sit). Align numbers on the decimal point, not the right edge: '3297 / 1689 / 858.4' and '26.39 / 6.851' are hard to compare as set. Add a direction cue for each unit (higher is better for GB/s and MB/s, lower for ns, µs and ms). Style the cells so they look like links, since the caption says each one links to its Series file but nothing shows it.
3. Settle the rounding contradiction. The project's stance is that figures are exact, and section 4.3 says 'This page changes only units, by moving the decimal point', with note 3 adding 'Nothing on this page is ... computed from the figures'. But Table 1 and Figure 1 round to four significant digits. Either show the exact p50 in the main table (Table S1 shows that digits grouped in threes, in mono, read well) or rewrite 4.3 and note 3 to say that Table 1 is rounded for reading and S1 is exact. As it stands, the page's own words are false about the page.
4. Rethink Figure 1 (desktop-light-01 to -02, about two screens). Zero-based linear scales are honest, but at this zoom most p5-p95 bars shrink to slivers. For a general reader the panels mostly redraw the medians already in Table 1, and the pale pink bars (light) and brown bars (dark) are low-contrast on top of that. Either merge spread into Table 1 (p5-p95 as a small inline bar or as numbers next to each median, so the medians aren't printed twice) or keep the panels but make them smaller, with darker spread bars and the count of Runs (n) beside each row. n is now visible only in Table S1.
5. Phone (phone-light-01 to -08, about 15,000 CSS px): much of the length comes from duplication. Each median appears in Table 1's per-benchmark lists and again in Figure 1. Choose one. The section 5 code block (phone-light-07) clips every curl URL at the right edge ('…/v1/index.', '…/v1/series'), which breaks the one thing a developer wants to copy: wrap the URLs or break them after '/v1/'. The Table 2 cards on phone are good; give Table 1 something equally deliberate, such as a compact per-machine toggle, rather than 14 stacked lists.
6. Show what you get. Section 5 and the Data availability box list addresses and schemas but never show a few lines of the JSON: one figure with its Method, version, n and Series id. An agent developer decides from that excerpt. Put one under the first curl.
7. Trim academic props that carry no information. 'Keywords', the envelope 'Correspondence:' that points to a JSON file (it reads as a contact address), the vertical arXiv-style stamp in the left margin, and nanosecond timestamps in the hero (keep them in Notes; show the hero to the minute) all add noise. Use the space to say who the page is for in the title deck. The phrase 'for agents and developers' is now buried in the sidebar and in the last sentence of the abstract.
8. Fix the benchmark descriptions that disagree with their units. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' says 'How many direct reads … completes', but the figure is µs per completed read. Check every row's description against its unit, in Table 1 and in the Figure 1 subtitles.

KEEP
The scientific-report concept, carried through with real care: numbered sections, footnotes, equations (1)-(3), a reference list that points into the API, and the supplementary table. It fits a project whose whole claim is 'a source for each number'. Keep the Data availability box with a copyable curl on the first screen, plus the First Run, Latest Run and Prices copied stamps and '6,335 counted, 0 failed'. Table S1 is excellent: every digit grouped in threes, n per Series, and a linked Series id per row; it is the best exact-figures presentation I've seen in this set. Keep Table 2 printing AWS's price and description verbatim, the quoted 'which Runs count' rule in section 4.5, the restrained cream-and-oxblood palette with a warm, legible dark mode, the STIX/Plex pairing with machine names in mono, and the phone card layout for Table 2.

FALSE OR MISLEADING
- Section 4.3 and note 3 claim the page only moves decimal points and computes nothing, yet Table 1 and Figure 1 round to four significant digits. Table 2's 'cheapest first' is also an ordering the page imposes.
- The 'Random 4 KiB reads' description ('how many reads') doesn't match its unit (µs).
- 'Correspondence: api.ledgermath.com/v1/index.json' with an envelope icon implies a contact channel; it is a data file.
- Nothing visible marks Table 1's figures as links, though the caption says each one links to its Series file.
- The disk rows (131.1 MB/s, 333.3 µs) are the same on every machine, probably because of the gp3 volume's provisioned limits. Footnote b names the gp3 root volume, but a reader comparing machines may still read those rows as machine performance. A one-line note would prevent that without interpreting the data.

v4.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Help the reader compare, which the board does not do yet. In desktop-light-00/01 every cell is the same black number. Nothing marks the best or worst machine in a row, there are no bars, and nothing says whether higher or lower is better beyond the small 'MEDIAN RATE/TIME' label. Mark the best value in each row (a yellow underline or a filled chip in the house style), and put a short 'higher is better' or 'lower is better' next to MEDIAN RATE/TIME. A thin in-cell bar scaled to the row would also work. Right now a reader has to do the comparison in their head 70 times.
2. Use one unit across each row. In CPU 06 (Sort 1 MiB), c8a.2xlarge shows '858.4 µs' between '3.297 ms', '1.689 ms' and '2.830 ms'. When you scan the row, 858.4 looks like the biggest number when it is actually the fastest. Pick the unit per benchmark (0.8584 ms), not per cell. The exact line underneath can keep every digit.
3. Show the spread. The section intro says each figure is a p50, and section 04 defines 5th/50th/95th percentiles, but the board shows no range anywhere. For a benchmark site, how noisy a figure is matters as much as the figure itself. Add p5–p95 in small type under the exact line, or as a whisker on the bar from change 1. It is the strongest trust signal this data has, and the page leaves it out.
4. Make the board half as tall. Each row is 150–210 px because the description, the 'One repetition' line and the config line all sit in the left column, while the five figure cells use only their top third and leave large empty white blocks (desktop-light-01, OS 08 and DSK 12 especially). Keep the title and one line of description in the row and move 'One repetition' and the config into a hover/expand or a footnote. The whole 14×5 board should fit in about 1.5 desktop screens, so a visitor can see all of it.
5. Explain the disk rows, or they will mislead. DSK 10 reads about 131.1 MB/s on every machine, which is 125 MiB/s, the gp3 default throughput. DSK 12 reads 333.3 µs everywhere, which is exactly 1/3000 s, the gp3 default IOPS. These rows measure the EBS volume's provisioned limits, not the machines. The page says 'root EBS gp3 volume' in the description, but a reader comparing machines will conclude 'disks are identical'. Add one sentence on the Disk band (for example 'every machine boots the same default gp3 root volume: 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, so these rows show the volume's limits'). It will make the project look sharper, not weaker.
6. Rethink the hero. On desktop the left half's h1 is the wordmark 'LEDGERMATH', which repeats the logo in the bar above it. The right half is a large flip clock that says one thing: newest Run 17:07. Make the h1 a statement ('Measured AWS server benchmarks, every Run kept') and shrink the clock into a strip, which frees room for a glimpse of real figures or a JSON response above the fold. On the phone (phone-light-00) the clock comes BEFORE the name and the explanation, so the first thing a phone visitor sees is a decorative clock with no context. Move it below the intro there.
7. Show what an agent gets back. Section 03 has the curl commands and the schema table, which is good, but no response. Add a short excerpt of index.json, or of one Series file, showing a figure with its Series address, so 'cite every figure' becomes something you can see. Also make the cells look like links (the intro says each figure links to its Series file, but nothing in a cell shows that), and show one Series URL on hover/focus.
8. Phone details. The board turns into 14 cards × 5 machine rows, about nine phone screens. Consider a sticky machine/benchmark switcher or collapsing each category. The shell block wraps URLs mid-path ('…/v1/' then 'index.json'), and the schema table breaks 'series-/list' and '<yyyy-mm-/dd>.json' (phone-light-06). Give the file column the width, or let the block scroll sideways.

KEEP
- The house style: yellow/black/cream, condensed uppercase display type, a monospace data voice, numbered sections. It feels like a ledger or a departures board, and it holds together in light and in dark. The dark mode (desktop-dark-*) is genuinely well done, not just inverted.
- The cell's structure: a large figure, the exact value with every digit underneath, the newest-Run time and the Run count. This is the right information in the right order.
- Machine column headers that carry vCPU, memory and $/h, ordered cheapest first. The machine cards that quote AWS's own price-list wording ('$0.096 per On Demand Linux m5.large Instance Hour') plus the dated price file link: excellent provenance.
- The category bands with coded IDs (MEM 01, CPU 05…) and colour rails.
- The Method printed verbatim, the 'failed Runs are kept and shown, never dropped' line, and Failed Runs 0 shown up top.
- On the phone, the board as a card per benchmark, with machines as right-aligned rows, is a real redesign, not a squeezed table.

READS AS FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- DSK 12's description says 'How many direct reads the gp3 volume completes…' (a rate), but the figure is a MEDIAN TIME in µs per read. The wording and the number disagree.
- The board intro says 'The large figure is rounded', and then the Method block ends with the quote 'Every number is exactly as the Methods' Derivations hold it.' Both can be true, but side by side they jar for a project that 'does not round'. Say that the exact value is the figure and the large one is a display aid.
- 'SERIES 187' in the hero stats, while the board shows 70 cells. That is unexplained jargon on the first screen, and the mismatch makes the reader wonder what is missing. Either explain it (groups and variants) or show the count that matches what is on the page.
- The disk rows that are identical across machines (see change 5) will be read as a machine finding when they are a volume setting.
- Two self-quotes styled as pull-quotes ('Version 1 only ever gains fields…' attributed to 'THE API, ON VERSIONING', and the closing quote with no attribution) read like invented testimonials. State them plainly instead.

v5.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Fix the hero figure's digit tail (desktop-light-00, phone-light-00). The red '2615200030773' next to the giant 12.50 reads as a separate 13-digit number, like an ID, not as the rest of 12.502615200030773. On the phone it ends up bottom-left, cut off from the 12.50 by white space, with GB/s on the right, which is worse. Make it look like a continuation: keep it on the same baseline as the '12.50', start it with a hairline or the leading '…', set it smaller and lighter, or print the full value once underneath as the table does. The page's whole claim is exact figures, so its headline number has to be readable without effort.
2. Give the hero figure a reason, or pick a figure that has one. 'm5.large reads memory at 12.50 GB/s' is the cheapest machine's least surprising number. A newcomer gets no comparison and no reason to care. The What/Where/From/Source strip is excellent, so keep it, but either pick a figure that shows what LedgerMath is for (a spread across the five machines, or a cost-per-unit figure built from the price file) or add one line of comparison beside it, e.g. the same benchmark on the other four machines as small numbers.
3. Make the table comparable, not just readable (desktop-light-00/01). The figures are left-aligned and set ragged: 0.8584 next to 3.297, 101.2 next to 76.68. Right-align or decimal-align each column with tabular figures. Mark each row 'higher is better' or 'lower is better' (rows switch between GB/s rates and ns/µs/ms times, and nothing says which way is good). Consider a quiet mark on the best cell in each row. At the moment a reader has to do every comparison in their head.
4. Show spread and Run count per cell, not only in the hero. Only the hero says '36 counted Runs'. Every other cell is a bare p50 with no count and no p10/p90 or range. That matters most where cells are nearly equal (Hash 101.2 vs 101.2, syscall 93.24 vs 93.24, the disk rows). A small 'n=36 · p10–p90' line under the full-precision digits would carry the 'judge afterwards' message into the table itself. Today the table only asserts.
5. Explain the disk rows as limits of the volume (desktop-light-01 'Disk'). Read a file sequentially is 131.1 MB/s on every machine, and Random 4 KiB, 64 in flight is 333.3 µs on every machine. Those are the root gp3 volume's default throughput and IOPS caps, not a property of the machine types. Without a one-line note at the group heading, an agent or developer will read them as 'all five machines have equal disks'. Also, 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' is described as 'How many direct reads … completes' but the figure is a time per completed read in µs. Make the description match the figure.
6. Cut the phone page's length by redesigning the table, not by stacking it (phone-light-00 to -05). Five full-width machine rows for each of 14 benchmarks makes about 10,000 px of identical blocks, and benchmarks can't be compared with each other. Use a compact 5-row grid with short machine labels, a sticky machine-name column, or one horizontally scrollable table with a pinned first column. Collapse the grey 'Median time of one repetition…' paragraph behind a disclosure. The per-benchmark card is clean, but the page's length isn't justified by what it shows.
7. Tighten section 02's stat strip (desktop-light-02). The five columns break the four-column grid used everywhere else. '10 November' and '19 November' wrap onto two cramped lines at display size while '17:07', '6,335' and '187' sit on one. Use one date format at one size (e.g. '10 Nov') or go back to four columns. The nanosecond timestamps under them are a nice touch, so keep them.
8. Agents section and hero curl (desktop-light-00 top right, desktop-light-02). The hero curl block breaks 'curl' onto its own line, so it doesn't look like one copyable command. Widen it or shorten the line, and add a copy button to every command block. Show what comes back: a 6–10 line excerpt of index.json or one series entry with its percentiles and Run links would answer 'what do I get' faster than the prose does. The Machines section (04) repeats the price row from the table header at display size; it could be half as tall.

WHAT IS STRONG AND MUST BE KEPT
- A clear point of view: Swiss/International-style grotesque, tight display headlines, one red accent used only for the hero figure and its matching table cell. It doesn't look like a template, and the restraint carries through in dark mode.
- The headline 'AWS machines, measured four times a day.' with the boot times in the header bar: the newcomer knows in seconds what this is and how fresh it is.
- The What / Where / From / Source strip under the hero: provenance attached to a figure, in four short cells.
- Big four-digit figure with every digit underneath, with units set small: the right answer to 'exact but scannable'.
- The Run → Series → Method → Figure glossary, and quoting AWS's own price string under each machine ("$0.096 per On Demand Linux m5.large Instance Hour"). That is provenance done well.
- Three labelled curl commands, the schema list and the 'Version 1 only ever gains fields' promise.

ANYTHING FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- The hero's digit tail reads as an unrelated number (see 1).
- The disk rows invite a wrong conclusion about the machines (see 5), and the '64 in flight' description says 'how many' over a time figure.
- Small consistency check: the stat strip says the oldest Run is 10 November 23:36, while the hero's Series runs '11 November to 19 November'. That may be correct (different Series), but a reader will notice it. Saying which Series starts when, or labelling the window as 'counted Runs', would head this off.
- The intro says 'every figure links to its Series file', but nothing in the table cells looks like a link (no underline, no hover cue visible). Either show that they are links or soften the claim.

STRONG, keep:

- The stat strip (newest Run to the nanosecond, 6,335 kept / 0 failed, 187 Series, oldest Run, prices copied) and the footer that repeats the snapshot time.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED:
- 'hover any figure for every digit' on a touch phone is untrue there.
- Four-significant-digit rounding in the cards sits uneasily with the project's no-rounding stance. It is disclosed, but the hero chart's printed values are rounded with no marker on the figures themselves.

Collapse the mono 'Median time of one repetition…' line behind a tap, or tighten the row height. On phone, the full-digit line sits to the left of the rounded figure, the reverse of desktop. Put it under the figure, as desktop does, so the two layouts read alike and the line can be shorter.
7. Settle on one display voice. The H1 is a bold grotesque, while every other heading (The same numbers, Point your agent here, The Methods) and the Q are a high-contrast serif. The top of the page looks as if it came from a different template than the rest. Set the H1 in the serif as well, or demote the serif.
8. The small grey mono metadata under each benchmark and the field paths in the answer table are about 10–11 px, light grey on cream. They are hard to read in light mode and only just legible in dark. Raise their size or contrast one step. Rename the 'Copy first line' button to say what it copies (for example 'Copy index URL'), or give each curl its own copy button.

KEEP
- The worked Q&A with numbered sources, and 'Every figure in the answer, as the files hold it' with the exact JSON field path, rate code and raw pricePerUnit string. This is the best provenance device I have seen for this kind of site. It shows, rather than claims, that every number has a source.
- The agent's restraint line ('I haven't compared machines or worked out a cost per sort'). It is honest and on-brand.
- The rounded large figure with the full-digit line beneath. It answers 'exact' and 'scannable' at once.
- The cited cell highlighted in the table, with the 'priced in the answer above' tie-in on the machine card. These threads connect the page.
- 'Point your agent here': curl lines, a ready-to-paste prompt and schema links. It is concrete and usable.
- The boot timeline and the Runs/Series/oldest/newest/prices-copied strip. It shows freshness without clutter.
- Warm paper with a rust accent, and a dark mode that holds up. Category labels (MEMORY, COMPUTE …) give the table rhythm.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- The Random 4 KiB description describes a rate while the figure is a time (see 4).
- Identical disk/S3 figures across machines, left unexplained, invite the false conclusion that the machines perform the same on I/O (see 3).
- 'The large figure is rounded to four digits' is stated openly, and every digit sits beneath it, so it is not misleading. The rounded figure is visually dominant, though, on a project that says it does not round. Keep the full digits as prominent as they are now, or more.
- No invented figures spotted: the Run counts (34 for one Series, 6,335 across 187 Series), the dates and the prices agree with each other across the sections.

v8.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Stop rounding the headline table by default (desktop-light-01, the line above the table: 'Rounded to four significant figures… Every digit' toggle off). The project's stance is exact figures, the hero card shows every digit, the JSON caption says 'nothing rounded', and the section is headed 'as measured'. Yet the main table, the thing most people compare, shows rounded values. Show the exact p50 by default in tabular mono, with digits past the fourth significant figure in a lighter tone if density is the worry. Then remove the toggle or flip it to 'Short form'. This fixes the page's one real contradiction at its cause.
2. Show the spread and the Run count in the table itself, not only on hover (desktop-light-01/02, every figure cell). Each cell already carries a dotted underline. Draw a thin p5–p95 whisker there, the same mark as the hero card's range bar, and add 'n=36' in the row's unit line or the column header. On phone, 'Hover a figure' does nothing (phone-light-03). Right now the table carries no sign of variance, so the trust story stops at the hero card.
3. Make the table denser and easier to compare. Rows are about 95–115 px tall on desktop because each one repeats a two-line description and a unit line. Fourteen rows take up most of two screens, and you cannot see Memory and Disk together. Put each description in a tooltip or in a single line in a lighter tone. Keep the unit and 'less/more is faster' as a small column. Mark the best figure in each row (bold or a rust dot) so the eye can scan for winners. Instances.vantage.sh shows how dense a figure table can get and still read well.
4. Say why the Disk figures are identical across all five machines (desktop-light-02, Disk group: 131.1 MB/s ×5, 333.3 µs ×5, ~900 µs ×5). These are the root EBS gp3 volume's baseline limits (125 MiB/s, 3,000 IOPS), not properties of the machines. i4i.2xlarge's local 1×1875 NVMe SSD, listed in its machine card, is never measured. Add a one-line group note ('all five read the same gp3 root volume, so these figures are its limits'). Without it, a reader or an agent will take these as machine comparisons.
5. On phone, the three curl commands look identical (phone-light-06, For agents section). Each one is cut to '$ curl https://api.ledgermath.com', so you cannot tell index, series and prices apart. On desktop the prices URL also runs under the Copy button (desktop-light-03). Wrap the command, or show the path first ('/v1/index.json', with the host in the label). Never truncate the part that tells the commands apart.
6. Phone table length (phone-light-03 to -06): 14 cards × 5 rows is roughly four tall screens of near-identical cards. Let the reader pick a machine to compare against, or use a compact 5-column grid with the machine names abbreviated in a sticky header row (m5.l / c8i.2xl …). Then a benchmark takes about 2 rows of height instead of a 400 px card. At minimum, add a jump list of the five groups at the table's top.
7. Give units one form across the machine cards (desktop-light-01, The machines). Network reads 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit', and Processor ranges from 'Intel Xeon Platinum 8175' to 'AMD EPYC 9R45 Processor'. If these are AWS's own strings, say so in the section caption. Otherwise put every network figure in Gbps and drop the repeated 'Processor'. The cards are also tall for five facts each: they could be a compact five-column spec table that lines up with the headline table's columns, which already carry vCPU and price.
8. Clear up the gap between the run schedule and the clock (desktop-light-00, middle stat). Boots happen at 04:10/10:10/16:10/22:10, yet the 'newest Run' is 17:07. Add 'Runs follow each boot one after another' or show the boot time beside the newest Run. Also say what the dial is: it reads as a 24-hour dial only once you notice the '00' and '12' labels.

KEEP
- The hero's split: a plain claim headline on the left and 'One figure, traced to its source' on the right. The card carries the exact digits, a correctly scaled p5/p50/p95 bar, counted and failed Runs, the date span, the setting, the Method, the zone and price, and the Series URL. It is the best single statement of what the project is, and it reads well on phone and in dark mode.
- The 'Newest Run started…' line under the CTAs, and the footer's nanosecond snapshot timestamp.
- The dark agent section: curl plus Copy, a one-line 'what you get' under each command, schema links, and the real JSON excerpt of the very Series shown at the top, with the 'nothing rounded' caption. The excerpt closing the loop with the hero is excellent.
- The 'A Method, versioned and written down' section, which quotes the definitions (R type 7 and so on) verbatim. Rare, and right for this audience.
- Plain-English benchmark names with a one-sentence description, an explicit unit and a 'less/more is faster' cue. The column headers carry vCPU and $/h.
- The type system (serif display, sans body, mono for identifiers) and a warm palette whose dark mode is done properly rather than inverted.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- 'Rounded to four significant figures' under a heading that says 'as measured', on a page whose JSON caption says 'nothing rounded'. See change 1.
- 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' is described as 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes', which is a count or rate, but the figure is 'µs per repetition, less is faster'. Make the description and the unit agree. 'Sort 1 MiB… How fast one core copies and sorts' against a time unit is a milder version of the same slip.
- The identical Disk figures look like machine results but are the volume's limits (change 4).
- The mutex footnote ('the decimal point moved four places') is accurate but reads like an admission that the figure was edited. Define the unit instead: ns per critical section, from 10,000 per repetition.
- 'Hover a figure for its percentiles' appears on phone, where you cannot hover.

ref:artificialanalysis.ai.notes: Intelligence, time and cost each get a chart with units or scoring direction, and the three distinct questions survive the move to stacked phone cards. Version notices and a dated changelog make revisions visible, though the angled model names are slow to match across charts and several later plots show only a legend and empty space in the captures.

ref:benchmark.clickhouse.com.notes: The title identifies the workload immediately, with methodology, reproduction and submission links close enough to inspect before accepting a ranking. The system filters consume the entire desktop first screen, and on the phone the ranked bars finally appear beneath a dense field of miniature orange labels.

ref:helix-db.com.notes: The account example pairs each match count with a source and a key, and the ticket example carries the explanation through to monthly totals and citations. The desktop hero offers agent setup, a sample company and a local option, while the phone directs a new reader to save the project for later and shrinks the product screenshot until its details are hard to read.

ref:instances.vantage.sh.notes: Region, billing period and precision sit directly above the instance rows, so a desktop reader can establish the basis of comparison at a glance. The MCP button and API announcement give developers two clear entry points, but on the phone that announcement covers rows in a viewport barely wide enough for the instance name.

ref:planetscale.com.notes: The latency chart has a percentile legend, a migration caption and a link to the benchmarks, giving the performance claim a concrete place to investigate. The opening customer grid delays that evidence by dozens of logos, especially on the phone where it wraps into two columns.

ref:turbopuffer.com.notes: The cache and object-store diagram turns vertically on the phone while preserving the read path, and the calculator keeps workload assumptions beside the monthly estimate. The latency panel names its workload, distinguishes warm and cold reads and links the benchmark, though the large difference between those readings is carried by very small labels.

ref:vercel.com.notes: The triangle and Deploy now button retain a clear order when the desktop composition becomes a phone stack. The Zapier example gives the scale claim a customer, a unit and a time period, but it takes considerable scrolling to get from the broad opening promise to that concrete use case.

v1.notes:
Changes, in priority order

1. Bring one actual comparison onto the first phone screen. In phone-light-00 the scope, command, metadata and reading instructions consume the viewport before a single result appears. Keep the copyable index and newest Run at the top. Move the boot timetable into the method section and replace the long reading instructions with an annotated first result. Seeing m5.large and c8a.2xlarge read the same buffer at different speeds would explain the ledger immediately.
2. Give the miniature plots a key. In desktop-light-00 the sequential-read row shows thin strokes of different lengths ending in dark marks of different widths. The adjacent prose names the percentiles, but leaves a reader to infer what each mark and the origin represent. Label one enlarged example with the actual median and percentile endpoints, and specify that only machines within that benchmark share a scale. Use that same key on the phone.
3. On phone-light-05 the developer section opens with a promise about the index, then spends most of a tile annotating a single Run. The index and Series commands follow in phone-light-06. Put the fetch sequence immediately after the introduction and let the annotated Run follow the command that retrieves its file. Readers can then follow the example in order.
4. On phone-light-01 through -05, keep a compact section jump within reach and identify the current benchmark when scrolling through its five machines. Phone-light-03 opens on loopback TCP figures with machine names and prices but no visible benchmark or unit until the next section. A slim current-benchmark header with its unit and a contents link would help someone arriving midway through this long ledger.
5. In desktop-dark-mid, strengthen the secondary digits and percentile endpoints slightly. The medians stand out well, but the small, fine-weight figures are hard to follow when reading across all five columns. Preserve the bold leading digits and the quieter treatment of the exact tail.

Keep

The desktop ledger is the strongest element. Repeated machine headers, consistent price order, units with a direction of improvement, and bold leading digits make widely different workloads comparable without sacrificing any recorded digits. Keep the Run-count links beside each figure. Keep the disk and S3 marginal notes exactly where the comparison happens; the shared gp3 explanation makes five nearly identical sequential-read results intelligible. The serif masthead, red margin rule and restrained double rules give the page an identifiable voice that carries through dark mode and the phone reflow.

Potentially misleading

The reading guide promises “three places in ink”; on desktop-light-00 the random-read entry 3.481409… has a bold prefix of 3.481 even though rounding to three decimals and taking the first three digits after the point are different operations. The distinction matters on entries such as 17.309783… . Say explicitly that the bold prefix is the start of the exact value; reserve the word “rounded” for the displayed percentile endpoints. No other claim stood out as invented from the screenshots.

v2.notes:
Changes, in priority order

1. On phone-light-00, put a “Compare benchmarks” jump beside the opening summary and keep the index curl visible. The current route to the first measured value passes three commands, nine status entries and a reading guide. Someone arriving for one disk measurement should be able to go straight to it.
2. In desktop-light-00, align each machine heading, its repeated section label and its column of medians to a common anchor. The m5.large heading sits visibly to the right of its first memory result. The drift is particularly costly for the two nearly identical c8 instance names.
3. In desktop-dark-mid and phone-dark-mid, brighten the percentile ranges, run counts and machine labels, and give the small text more size. The amber units are easy to find, but the 585–700.6 range under the c8i disk read is more consequential to a comparison and much harder to pick out.
4. In the data rows, give the linked medians a consistent, subtle link cue visible at rest. In phone-light-01 the rust-coloured “[+] exact” is the obvious action, while the number that leads to the evidence looks like plain text. Rename the disclosure “Exact p5–p95” so its scope is clear after the introduction has scrolled away.
5. In the disk section of desktop-light-01 and phone-light-03, rewrite the random-read description to say what the reported microseconds measure with 64 reads outstanding. State whether the value is elapsed time divided by completions or the latency of an individual request. The distinction matters to someone using the figure in an estimate.

Keep the manual-page structure, especially the pairing of NAME with executable examples under SYNOPSIS. The commands name their payloads, the freshness and failure counts are explicit, and the methods explain the calculation all the way down to how an even-sized median is taken. Keep the five-machine order across sections, the full median with its leading digits emphasised, and the phone layout that puts the machine name next to every value. The gp3 explanation belongs directly above the disk figures, where it prevents a mistaken inference about the i4i instance store.

Potentially misleading wording: “How many direct reads” promises a count or rate while the row reports µs and a downward arrow. Also, “Every digit printed” in DATA appears to cover the short p5–p95 ranges as well as the medians. Specify that every median digit is visible and that the disclosure supplies the full range endpoints.

v3.notes:
Changes, highest value first

1. On phone-light-00, put the exact memory-read example and copyable index address directly beneath the subtitle. The five superscripted machine names, shared footnote, timestamps and repeated description currently push both payoffs below the first screen. Keep the latest Run and count beside the example.
2. Give Results an obvious “Show exact figures” control beside the caption on desktop-light-00 and phone-light-00. In the sequential disk-read panel on phone-light-02 four medians read 131.1. The exact supplement distinguishes them, but a reader has to remember the row-selection instruction or find the appendix. Open the chosen benchmark’s five exact medians together for comparison.
3. Add a compact benchmark jump menu above Figure 1 on phone-light-00, grouped by the same Memory, Compute, Operating system, Disk and Network headings used on desktop. Someone looking for S3 currently passes thirteen panels before reaching it.
4. Enlarge the p5, p95 and Run-count labels in Figure 1 on desktop-light-01 and put them above their columns. A reader has to look below the fifth machine to interpret the first row. Preserve the bold median and the shared scale within each panel.
5. On phone-light-04, show a short excerpt of Listing 1 by default, pairing the highlighted bytes_per_second.p50 with its exact GB/s equivalent. Offer the full object inline on demand. That would make the worked example easier to reproduce and shorten the path to the schema links.

Keep the dated report masthead, warm paper and ink palette, and restrained dark treatment. The lettered panels, repetition definitions and direction arrows let readers compare machines while keeping the task and unit in view. The abstract’s exact value, sample count and Series ID, followed through into the marked JSON field, give the API a concrete purpose. Table S1’s grouped digits and bold p50 column make unusually long values tractable.

Potentially misleading: phone-light-00 cites “Table 1a” although the phone Results section presents Figure 1(a). Point that citation to the visible panel. Note 3 on phone-light-06 says nothing on the page is computed from the figures, while the mutex note explicitly divides a repetition across 10,000 critical sections. Describe the scope precisely: the page converts units and reports per-section time without aggregating across machines.

v4.notes:
Changes, in priority order
1. On phone-light-00, bring the first actual measurement up. The newest Run appears in a strip, a flip clock, a full timestamp and a timeline marker before the reader sees a single result. Keep the strip, add us-east-2 there, and put the schedule and clock behind a “Round details” control. Keep the full clock on desktop, where it sits beside the introduction.
2. On phone-light-02 through -04, give the percentile interval enough room to stay on one line. In the SHA and random-read cards the interval breaks immediately after the hyphen, while the long exact median sits in a separate column in very small type. Give the exact value, with its unit, a line beneath the large median and use the recovered width for a consistently labelled p5–p95 interval. This would also help the low-contrast secondary figures in phone-dark-mid.
3. In the board legend on desktop-light-00 and phone-light-00, label the time badge as “latest Run start (UTC)” and state that each benchmark has its own bar scale. The explanation after the last row comes too late. Especially on phone, 16:22 beside 36 Runs could easily be read as the time all those observations were collected.
4. Compress the five consecutive phone machine cards (phone-light-05/06). Start with a five-row comparison of name, hourly price, vCPU and RAM. Let each row reveal its CPU model, network, storage, AWS billing wording and identifiers. The current layout makes comparing the first and fifth prices a scrolling exercise.
5. On phone-light-06, make the worked evidence address a visible link or give it its own copy control beside the JSON excerpt. The shell commands have clear copy affordances, but following the example from a Series down to one Run appears to require selecting a long wrapped string.

Keep the departure-board identity, the five price-ordered desktop columns, and the matched order in the phone cards. The short median plus full digits makes both scanning and transcription possible. Keep the disk-specific interpretation directly above the affected rows. The highlighted mutex sample, its Series median and the matching board row give the API section a concrete teaching example worth preserving.

Potentially misleading wording: the note after the board on phone-light-04 says to hover or focus for every digit even though the complete value is already printed on each card. Point to the printed value on touch screens. No other apparent factual contradiction in the screenshots.

v5.notes:
Changes, in priority order

1. Carry one measurement through both API examples (desktop-light-03, phone-light-06). Step 1 opens the highlighted m5.large memory Series, then step 2 shows a mutex Run on c8i.2xlarge. Show an actual point from the Series just opened, with the matching machine, unit and evidence address. A developer should be able to follow both reads in order and recognize the result.
2. Repeat the five machine headings at each desktop benchmark group. In desktop-light-01 and desktop-dark-mid, five precise measurements sit across each row with no visible clue which machine owns which column. Short repeated headings would also work for readers arriving directly from the benchmark index.
3. Give exact values and percentile ranges more legible type in the desktop matrix, particularly in dark mode. In the sequential file-read row four machines show 131.1 MB/s. The tiny line below each headline is where their differences can actually be read. There is room to enlarge it within the current columns.
4. Keep the benchmark index within reach on the phone. A small category jump control or return link at each group heading would let a reader halfway through Disk reach Network or the API without retracing several screens. Keep the five machine rows visible together.
5. In the API examples on phone-light-06, wrap the long evidence addresses or give each example a visible copy control. Their right ends disappear at the code block boundary, precisely where the reader needs the evidence link.

Keep the single red measurement tied to a machine, benchmark, exact value and count. The adjacent five-bar comparison immediately gives the magnitude context. The right-aligned five-machine groups on the phone are particularly successful. Keep the plain-language description of a repetition, direction of improvement, dated prices and copyable index request.

Potentially misleading: the two-read walkthrough switches Series as described above. Also qualify “Nothing rounded” in the Figure definition as a property of the stored value. The largest type on the page is explicitly a rounded display value.

v6.notes:
Changes, in priority order
1. Put the counted Run total for each machine beside its median in the instrument charts (desktop-light-00/01, phone-light-02 onward). The hero teaches the reader that 33 Runs support 19.58 GB/s. That context disappears in the very next comparison. The site-wide 6,335 cannot answer the same question for another dot.
2. Bring the phone benchmark index closer to the first screen (phone-light-00/01). The compact two-column list is an excellent way to choose a measurement, but reaching it means passing the worked example and freshness panel. Give the first-screen benchmark link an explicit destination such as ‘Choose a benchmark’ and add a return link at the end of each chart group so a second lookup takes one jump.
3. Give the phone ‘Every digit’ table a machine selector above the values (phone-light-05/06). At the starting position a whole column of exact figures fits, plus fragments of the next column. Choosing two named machines would make a comparison across distant columns possible without remembering a 16-digit number while swiping. Preserve the full matrix on desktop.
4. Raise the size and contrast of axis ticks, units, percentile labels and settings throughout the chart grid, particularly in desktop-dark-top and phone-dark-mid. The orange dots and bright medians read immediately, but the smaller gray text needed to interpret them recedes. Spend some of the space on the settings rows on those labels.
5. In the worked Run near the bottom (desktop-light-04, phone-light-09), use the sequential memory-read Series from the hero and API example, or label the mutex example as a new case. Following one published median all the way to one contributing Run would make the provenance chain easier to verify.

Keep the first-screen pairing of a precise claim, a copyable index request and an actual measured distribution. The worked chart explains the dot, whisker, machine, exact digits and source together. Keep the consistent price ordering across all instruments, the explicit faster direction, and especially the miniature zero-based context above a zoomed axis. The restrained warm paper, fine rules and orange marks give this a recognizable identity in both themes. The API example ties an actual response field back to the number on the page.

Potentially misleading: ‘Every digit’ introduces the table as the same 70 figures as the charts, while the table shows exact values and the charts print medians to four or six significant digits. The chart headings do disclose precision, but ‘70 exact medians, shown rounded in the charts’ would resolve the distinction at the point of comparison. No visibly invented measurements.

v7.notes:
Changes, in priority order
1. In the phone comparison section (phone-light-01 to -05), put a compact benchmark jump menu beside the section heading. A reader looking for a disk latency currently passes every memory, compute and operating-system result. Preserve the five-machine stacks once the reader arrives.
2. At the top of the Q&A (desktop-light-00 and phone-light-00), shorten the question and put the median sort time and hourly rate together on the first answer line. Then give the sample size, dates and percentile interval. On the phone the first screen reaches the question before it gives the visitor a measured result.
3. Give the comparison bars a small illustrated key at the start of the matrix. In desktop-dark-mid and phone-dark-mid the solid stroke and end tick are clear, but the percentile band nearly disappears where the five disk measurements cluster. Give the band stronger contrast and make the exact p5 and p95 readable on demand for each median.
4. Replace the relative GET path in the masthead facts strip with a copyable absolute index URL. The first screen currently splits the host and path between two places, while the ready-to-copy command is below all fourteen benchmarks (desktop-light-02 and phone-light-06).
5. Label the two columns of the example evidence table in desktop-light-00 with their respective units or roles. The sort field is stored in nanoseconds, while the displayed value is in microseconds. Make that conversion explicit beside the first pair so a developer can reproduce it without counting decimal places.

Keep
The question, numbered sources, highlighted sort cell and highlighted machine price form a continuous, checkable example. Keep the bolder leading digits within each exact value, repeated machine headings, direction and unit on each benchmark, and the run count immediately under each figure. The disk and S3 notes explain what the measurements can actually distinguish. The editorial type and restrained rust accent work in both themes.

Potentially misleading
The evidence table promises figures “as the files hold it” even where the displayed value is converted from ns to µs.

v8.notes:
Changes, in priority order

1. Carry one example all the way to its evidence. In desktop-light-03 and phone-light-07 the JSON excerpt continues the hero’s sequential memory read on m5.large, but the panel immediately below jumps to a mutex on c8i.2xlarge. Use a counted Run from the featured Series there. A reader could then follow the same machine, benchmark and Series ID from headline to boot record.
2. Bring the worked number onto the first phone screen. In phone-light-00 the headline, paragraph, two full-width actions and freshness line consume the viewport before the example starts. Keep the headline and timestamp, shorten the introduction to a sentence, and put the exact median and its 36 counted Runs directly beneath it. This lets the figure demonstrate the promise before the reader scrolls.
3. Explain the range plots where the table begins (desktop-light-01, phone-light-02/03). The prose identifies p5–p95, but leaves the pale baseline and its scale unexplained. Label a single example with the axis limits, median marker and whisker ends, and say which machines share a scale. This matters most on phone, where five plots line up vertically and invite direct comparison.
4. Keep machine names in view throughout the desktop table. In desktop-light-02 the disk and network rows give five precise answers with no visible instance names. Repeat the column headings at each section break or keep them pinned while scrolling.
5. Give the trailing digits in the results a little more contrast, especially in desktop-dark-mid and phone-dark-mid. Preserve the darker or bolder leading digits for scanning. In the hero, reduce the extreme size change after ‘12.50’ so the suffix reads as part of the same number.
6. Normalize the network specification for comparison (desktop-light-01, phone-light-02). Show 10 Gigabit and 15000 Megabit in the same unit, retaining AWS’s ‘up to’ qualification and its original wording in the linked source.

Keep the side-by-side headline and worked receipt on desktop. The legible p5/p50/p95 diagram, sample window, configuration, counted and failed totals, and direct Series address answer real questions about one measurement in very little space. Keep the phone’s five labeled machine rows per benchmark, the faster-direction labels beside the units, and the API section’s three distinct copyable requests with descriptions of what comes back. The warm paper, serif headings and restrained orange carry through to the boot-to-API illustrations and the dark theme.

Potentially misleading: ‘One step further: a Run inside a Series file’ below the featured Series excerpt suggests the Run belongs to that Series. The small print identifies the switch to a different benchmark. The screenshots give no other clear reason to call a claim invented.

ref:artificialanalysis.ai.notes: A clear claim, 'Independent analysis of AI', in a confident serif, with the three headline metrics (intelligence, time, cost per task) shown as labelled, value-on-bar charts on the first screen. A dated changelog signals freshness. The rotated model labels are hard to read, especially on phone; the many provider hues make comparison harder rather than easier; and the way in for a developer or an agent isn't on the home page. In this capture most charts further down are blank (they load lazily), which leaves long empty boxes.

ref:benchmark.clickhouse.com.notes: An honest benchmark page. Methodology, 'Reproduce and Validate the Results', a JSON benchmark and Add a System are the first links you see, and each result row carries its own date, category tag and a relative multiplier (×1.62) in an aligned column. Its main fault is that the filter wall of hundreds of beige chips takes the whole first screen on desktop, and nearly two screens on phone, before any result shows. The type and colour are default-browser utilitarian, with little hierarchy beyond the H1.

ref:helix-db.com.notes: A distinct, consistent identity: a dotted pixel display face, mono body text, warm paper colours, corner-bracket buttons. The way in for agents and developers is the primary action ('Set up with your agent', a copyable 'run it locally'). Provenance is shown, not claimed: '60 of 62' match bars, sources named for each field, an example answer with footnoted citations and monthly counts. The mono body text on a long line is slow to read, and the beige-on-beige panels are low in contrast. The phone page is designed: it says honestly that the product needs a bigger screen and offers a GitHub star instead.

ref:instances.vantage.sh.notes: The densest, most directly useful figure table of the set: exact CoreMark scores, monospaced API names, filters on every column, region and price-unit controls right where you need them. It costs a lot: numbers are left-aligned and don't share a precision (95,158.796 next to 192,539.11), the 'Updated' line is hidden under a cookie banner and a promo pop-up covers the table, and nothing says where a score comes from or how many runs are behind it. The phone page is the desktop table cut off at the right edge, which is not a design.

ref:planetscale.com.notes: A strong, consistent point of view: all-monospace prose, hairline-ruled logo grid, ASCII-style diagrams, dotted section rules. It reads like engineers wrote it, and the p50/p95/p99 before-and-after graph links on to a benchmarking page. But the first screen is a wall of mono paragraphs with no single big claim, the logo grid takes several screens (worse on phone, where it runs to two columns of dozens of cells), and there are few figures for a page that sells speed.

ref:turbopuffer.com.notes: The best of the set at turning figures into the pitch. A plain claim ('search every byte'), a small architecture diagram, a scale line (1T+ documents, 10M+ writes/s), then a working cost calculator and p50/p90/p99 bars for warm and cold namespaces, with the workload stated and the benchmark repo linked, plus a limits table that gives 'seen in prod' next to each limit. The dark-to-light bands, pixel-shadowed boxes and mono type are carried through with care. On phone it reflows well, though the limits table wraps awkwardly. A developer has no command or snippet on the home page.

ref:vercel.com.notes: Excellent type and restraint (the tight grotesk headline, the generous whitespace), but 'Agentic Infrastructure' with a triangle says little to a newcomer in ten seconds, and the page has almost no figures besides a customer stat. In this headless capture everything below the first section is blank (scroll-triggered content never appeared), so most of the page's length was empty: in practice it is a polished template with not enough said.

v1.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Make the table rows shorter (desktop-light-00 and -01, every row). Each row is about 130 px tall because the left column holds the title, the description and the italic spec line ('Bytes per second. 1 GiB, one thread, AVX2 loads, static build.'). The five figure cells use only the top ~60 px of that, so the 14x5 ledger runs to about 2.5 desktop screens with a band of empty space under every row of numbers. Keep the title and one line of description, and put the spec line behind a disclosure or into the Series file. Aim for about 70 px a row, so a whole section fits on one screen and the eye can move down a column. The same fix shortens the phone page.
2. Help the reader compare across a row without adding any computed figure. Today, picking the winner of a row means reading five 15-digit numbers. The rule bars are drawn from zero, so the rows where the machines are nearly equal (10, 12, 13, 14) show five identical bars and say nothing. Mark the best cell in each row according to its direction (a small mark, or keep the 'ink' weight for the leader only), and think about scaling each bar to the row's own min-max rather than from zero. The direction note '↑ higher is better' is small grey italic under the unit; it carries a lot of weight for its size.
3. Give the masthead (desktop-light-00 top, phone-light-00 top) one statement at display size before the paragraph. Right now the wordmark and tagline are followed by five lines of body text all in one weight, and the reader has to dig out what this is from it: measured AWS performance, every Run kept, static JSON for agents. 'A book of record for cloud servers' is a good line but it is poetic; a newcomer needs the plain sentence above the fold too. The metadata block on the right (newest Run, Runs, boot times) is excellent; keep it.
4. Typeset the pencil digits as a fixed grid. Group the digits by three from the decimal point and give the tail a fixed width in tabular figures, so that every median in a column lines up on its decimal point. Today the tails end ragged ('016 3', '312 7', '016 25' next to '877'), and in some rows the bold part is indented to line up while in others it is not (row 14 compared with row 10). An exact figure is the whole point of the page, so its alignment should be faultless.
5. Repeat the machine header, with price and vCPU, while scrolling (desktop). The small mono machine names repeated at each section break are good, but once you are past the first screen nothing tells you which column costs $0.096 and which costs $1.36, and price is half of any decision this page serves. If the header is already sticky, ignore this; a static screenshot cannot show it.
6. Phone (phone-light-00 to -07): the cards are properly designed, but the page is about 15 screens long and the ledger alone is about 10. Add a compact mode (hide descriptions and spec lines), or a sticky jump bar for the five sections. The curl command breaks over three lines ('$ curl / https://api.ledgermath.com/v1/ / index.json'), so it reads as three commands; let it scroll sideways on one line, or show the short address and let COPY carry the full command.
7. Give the oxblood red one job. It is used at once for section labels, the N.B. notes, the left rule of the code blocks, the double rule beside the figure column on phone and the border of the sample Run. Red italic N.B. text reads as an error or a warning, when these notes are explanations (the EBS throughput limit, the IOPS limit). Set the N.B. text in ink and keep only a red marker. In dark mode the salmon is fine, but the same overuse applies.
8. In 'For agents and developers', the 'One Run, as its Series' file gives it' panel is a list of fields annotated in prose, not JSON anyone could copy. Next to it, show a short excerpt of a real index.json or Series response, as monospace JSON with a COPY button, and say what the request returns (size, how often it changes). The four curl rows are already very good.

KEEP
The ledger idea, carried right through: three places in ink and the rest in pencil, roman-numeral sections, double rules, N.B. notes, the colophon naming the faces. It is the most distinctive point of view among the pages I calibrated against, and none of it reads as a template. Keep the 'N Runs ↗' link in every cell that opens the evidence, the honest N.B. notes on the rows limited by EBS and S3, the price and vCPU in the column headers, the AWS price quoted in AWS's own words, the 'How a figure is kept' glossary with Series 187, Runs 6,335, counted 6,335 and failed 0, and oldest and newest Run to the nanosecond. Keep the copyable curl in the first screen with 'How agents read it ↓', the four documented endpoints, and the evidence URL pattern. On phone, keep the card per benchmark with a mini-table per machine; it is a real redesign, not the desktop page squeezed. The dark mode is faithful to the light one.

FALSE OR MISLEADING
- Row 12 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight': the description says 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes', which is a count or rate, but the figure is µs per completed read, lower is better. The N.B. says this, but the description contradicts it. Rewrite it as a time.
- The masthead says each figure is printed 'to every digit', and the project does not round, yet the p5-p95 range under every figure is rounded to three places (the footnote admits it). Either print the ranges exactly as well, or say 'range rounded' where the range is shown, not only in a footnote below the table.
- The masthead's '6,335 in 187 Series' sits above a table of 70 Series whose cells show about 33 to 36 Runs each. That is reconciled only in the footnote. Say 'this table: 70 of 187 Series' near the ledger heading.
- Rows 06 ('How fast one core copies and sorts') and 01 to 04 ('How fast...') are fine. Row 10 says 'Bytes per second' while the unit is MB/s. That is consistent, but a reader may wonder whether MB means 10^6 or 2^20; say which.

v2.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Make cross-machine comparison visible, not something you have to read for. In every DATA row (desktop-light-00/01, phone-light-01..05) all five figures look the same weight, so finding the best machine for a benchmark means reading 5 long numbers. Mark the best figure in each row (and maybe the worst) with one quiet device: the accent colour on the bold digits, a small marker, or a hairline bar under each figure scaled to the row. That fixes the cause; at present the table is a very good record and a weak comparison tool.
2. Put a figure in the first screen. On desktop (desktop-light-00, top 900 px) the first row of numbers sits exactly on the fold at y~870; on phone (phone-light-00, top 1688 px) there is not one benchmark figure on the first screen. Tighten the space above DATA (the DATA intro paragraph and the jump-link row can be shorter, and STATUS could be two lines) so at least the whole MEMORY first row shows on desktop, and on phone lead with one row of real figures before or right after SYNOPSIS.
3. Give DATA the hierarchy it deserves. NAME, SYNOPSIS, STATUS, DATA, SEE ALSO are all the same small bold caps; DATA is the reason the page exists and reads as one section among ten. Keep the man-page labels but let the benchmark groups and the machine column header carry more weight. The machine header repeated above COMPUTE, OS, DISK and NETWORK is tiny pale grey (desktop-light-00 y~1435, -01 y~587, y~1223) and is hard to read; make it the same style as the top header (name + vCPU/GiB + $/h), or make that header sticky.
4. Cut the prose between the figures. Each benchmark carries a title, a description, an italic 'one repetition' line and a 'setting' line before its numbers (two or three lines on desktop, four to six on phone, e.g. phone-light-02 'Lock and unlock a mutex'). Keep the title and the one-line description visible; move 'one repetition' and 'setting' behind [+] with the exact digits. That alone would shorten the phone page by perhaps a third and let the figures dominate.
5. Make ranges consistent and the links visible. p5-p95 precision varies within a row: 'Read a file sequentially' shows 131.27-131.33 next to 131.1-131.2; 'Hash 64 bytes' shows 101.1-101.4 next to 76.64-77.18. Pick one rule (same significant digits as the bold part of the p50) and keep trailing zeros. Also, the text says 'each figure links to its Series file' but the figures carry no link affordance at all in the shots; give them a faint underline or a dotted rule so the evidence link is discoverable.
6. Fix the phone STATUS order. On phone-light-00 the three desktop columns are flattened row by row, so it reads newest, where, runs, oldest, series, schedule, prices... newest and oldest are separated, and wraps like 'UTC' alone on a line and '0 / failed' are awkward. Reorder for one column (newest, oldest, runs, series, schedule, prices, where, methods, evidence) and drop the fractional seconds on phone or let them sit in grey on the same line.
7. Show what an agent gets back. SYNOPSIS gives the three curl commands with copy buttons, which is excellent, but nowhere does the page show a few lines of the JSON a Series file returns (a figure, its n, its p5/p95, the Run link). A 6-10 line excerpt under SYNOPSIS or in FILES would make 'cite the file behind each number' concrete. Also the third command hard-codes prices/2026-11-19.json, which goes stale tomorrow; offer a stable 'latest' address if the API has one, or say the date changes daily.
8. Lift the small greys. 'p5-p95 n' labels, range text, 'n=34' and the repeated machine headers are ~11 px mid-grey on cream; they are likely below comfortable contrast, especially the light-mode range lines. Darken them a step in light mode; the dark mode is already better here.

KEEP. The man-page concept (LEDGERMATH(5), NAME/SYNOPSIS/STATUS/EXIT STATUS/FILES/SEE ALSO) is a genuine point of view, apt for a data format and its developer readers, and it is carried through to the footer; 'EXIT STATUS: 0 Runs failed of 6,335' is a lovely touch. Bold leading digits with the full exact tail in grey is the right answer to 'never round' and should stay. Decimal-aligned figures, the unit and higher/lower arrow at the start of each row, n per cell, the p50 header with vCPU/GiB/$/h per machine. STATUS (newest/oldest to the nanosecond, runs kept/counted/failed, schedule, zone, '187, 70 of them in DATA below') is honest and dense without clutter. The DISK note that these rows measure the EBS root volume, not the i4i instance store, is exactly the kind of candour that builds trust. METHODS spelled out in full (R type 7, what 'counted' means). The phone curl commands wrapped with a trailing backslash, and the phone machine cards. Both colour modes are warm and coherent.

FALSE OR MISLEADING. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' is described as 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes' but the figure is in microseconds, lower is better (333.3 us): the description promises a count/rate and the number is a time per completed read. Say 'the time per completed read' or show IOPS. 'Every digit printed' sits above ranges that are rounded to four or five digits; the [+] exact explanation covers it, but the sentence should say the p50 is printed in full and the ranges are shortened. The METHODS 'counted' paragraph cites 'scripts/check-events.py' and '--quick stream' with no link or explanation, which reads as internal repository jargon to a visitor. The page header 'LedgerMath Data API' presents the home page as the API's page; minor, but the API is one part of what the page offers.

v3.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Stop showing the same 70 medians three times. Table 1 (rounded p50, desktop-light-00), Figure 1 (the same p50s again plus p5/p95/n, desktop-light-01) and Table S1 (exact, desktop-light-03/04) are one dataset printed three ways, and they make up most of a desktop page of roughly 8,000 px. Merge Table 1 and Figure 1 into one table: each cell holds the median, a small 5-95 range mark and n, so it can be scanned and compared without hunting for the spread in a separate figure. Keep S1 as the full-precision appendix, or drop it once the main table is exact (see 2).
2. Resolve the conflict with the project's stance on exactness. The project does not round, yet the headline table and the figure round to four significant digits. Exact digits appear only in the abstract's one example and in S1, which is collapsed on the phone. Show every digit in the main table instead, grouped in threes as S1 already does well, with the leading significant digits in full weight and the tail lighter and smaller. That keeps the table exact and still scannable, and it removes the need for the rounding disclaimers that now fill three captions and §4.3.
3. Figure 1's caption says it shows "the spread", but on linear axes that start at zero the 5th-95th bars are invisible or a few pixels wide in most panels (a, b, e, g, j, l, n), so the figure actually shows magnitude. Either call it a magnitude comparison, or show spread so it can be seen: for example the p5-p95 width as a percentage of the median, or a zoomed axis per panel. The zero-based bars also show five identical ticks for j and l. Say on the row itself why all machines read 131 MB/s and 333 µs (the same gp3 root volume) instead of leaving that to footnote b.
4. The masthead (desktop-light-00 top, phone-light-00 top) has no way out: no Docs, no API, no source repository, though this is an open-source developer tool. The docs link appears only as Reference [6] near the bottom. Add a short nav (API · Docs · Source · Methods) to the right of the snapshot date.
5. Clean up the reference apparatus and tighten the hero. The machine list puts five identical superscript 1s after the names, and then a different "note 1" (Notes, desktop-light-03) is cited from §4.1. Table notes a-c and references [1]-[6] add two more systems. Number the notes uniquely and replace the five 1s with a plain region line. The hero (title, italic subtitle, machine list, footnote, freshness strip) uses about 330 px, so on desktop Table 1's first row sits exactly at the 900 px fold. Trim it so at least four rows of figures show on the first screen.
6. Phone: Listing 1 (phone-light-04) soft-wraps long JSON lines to column 0. It breaks the URL mid-id ("a0faf4326 / dd7.json") and wrecks the indentation, which is the one place an agent developer looks for structure. Give the block horizontal scroll, or show a trimmed listing on narrow screens. The phone page is also about 12,000 CSS px long. Collapse §4.4-4.5 (equations, the long counted-rule quote), Notes and References behind disclosures the way S1 already is.
