7. Table 2's "AWS's description" column (desktop-light-01/02, and the italic line on each phone card) repeats the price word for word on every row. One sentence saying prices are printed as AWS's file words them [3] does the same job. In §4 on desktop (desktop-light-02/03, 4.1-4.3) narrow justified columns open rivers ("This snapshot holds 187 Series and 6,335 Runs: 6,335"). Set them ragged-right.
8. Table 1's columns are ragged. Decimal alignment combined with four significant digits makes the decimal point move around (column 1 of row f, "3297", hangs left of the others, and column b drifts), and a dotted underline under every one of the 70 cells adds texture that competes with the digits. Use a fixed precision per row so each column right-aligns cleanly, and show the link affordance only on hover or focus.

WHAT IS STRONG AND MUST BE KEPT
- The data-report point of view. It is carried all the way through (abstract, numbered sections, Listing, References, colophon naming the typefaces), it is unlike every reference, and it fits a project whose claim is rigour. STIX Two Text with IBM Plex Mono is a good pairing.
- The freshness strip under the title (First Run, Latest Run, Prices copied, Runs 6,335 counted, 0 failed), and on the phone the same strip as a definition list.
- The Data availability box on the first screen, with a copyable curl to index.json and the two main files beside it.
- The abstract's one exact example tied to its Series id and its count of Runs.
- Listing 1. The highlighted "p50" that maps Table 1's first figure to a JSON path is the best agent-facing detail on any of these pages. Keep Table 3 with its schema links too.
- §4: the published equations, the counted-rule quoted word for word, and the Series ids beside every exact figure in S1. S1's digit grouping in thin-space threes.
- The phone adaptations are real design, not squeezing: Table 1 is replaced by the panels, Table 2 becomes cards, Table 3 becomes a stacked list, and S1 is collapsed.
- The warm dark mode, which keeps the same hierarchy, and the restrained use of a single accent.

ANYTHING FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- Note 3 says "Nothing on this page is averaged or computed from the figures", yet Table 1 and Figure 1 round every figure. That is disclosed, but the sentence overclaims. Rounding is computation, and it sits against the project's rule of no rounding.
- Figure 1 is captioned as showing spread while it mostly cannot show it (item 3).
- The hero says machines are booted at 04:10, 10:10, 16:10 and 22:10 UTC and the benchmarks run "while it is freshly booted". The Run times shown are 1 to 3.5 hours after the nearest boot (First Run 23:36, Latest Run 17:07, and Listing 1's oldest_run_started_at 13:44:51). A careful reader will ask what "freshly" means. Explain the gap on the page, or check the data.
- Two different footnotes are both numbered 1 (item 5), so a reader following a superscript can land on the wrong one.
- The rotated vertical stamp in the left margin is borrowed from the look of preprint servers. That is fine as a genre sign but not original, and on the first screen it reads as decoration.

v4.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Give the flip clock's space to the figures (desktop-light-00, right half of the hero; phone-light-00, the dark panel under the stats). On desktop the first 900 px hold no measured figure at all: the board's column headers appear at about y=790 and the first value at about y=950. Almost all of that space goes to one fact, the time the newest Run started, shown three times (the flip digits, the nanosecond timestamp, the green 'Newest Run 17:07:23' tag on the timeline). On the phone the same fact is shown a fourth time: the pill under the headline already says 'Newest Run 17:07 UTC', then about 550 CSS px of panel repeat it. Shrink the clock to a compact strip (newest Run, the four round times, the prices link) and use the space you gain for a live slice of the board: one row with all five machines, or the five machine headers with their prices and one figure each. The page's argument is its numbers, and a visitor should see one before scrolling.
2. Demote the per-cell time chips (all board rows, desktop-light-00/01). Each cell stacks five lines, and after the big figure its heaviest mark is a solid black '16:22' chip. There are 70 of them, nearly identical, and they shout louder than the p5-p95 range, which carries more information but sits in the faintest, smallest grey type on the page. Make the time plain secondary text, or state the range once per column ('newest Runs 16:12-16:23'), and raise the p5-p95 line's size and contrast. The cell would then read: figure, every digit, spread, Runs.
3. Say which machine is best on each row. Bars are scaled per row and drawn identically whether the row is '▲ higher is faster' or '▼ lower is faster', so a long bar means best in MEM and worst in CPU/OS/DSK/NET. The arrow chip is there, but the eye follows the bars. Mark the best figure on each row (weight, a dot, or the category colour), or draw every bar so that longer means better. Comparison is the board's whole job.
4. Fix the wrapped ranges on the phone (phone-light-02/03/04: CPU 05, OS 07, DSK 10, DSK 12). The p5-p95 text breaks onto two lines ('553.87-' / '573.71') beside the bar, so the rows lose their rhythm. Move the range under the full-digit line, or narrow the bar so the range fits on one line.
5. Turn the legend strip above the board into a real key (desktop-light-00 y≈767, phone-light-00 bottom). '12.50 GB/s enough digits to tell the row apart · 12.502615200030773 every digit the API holds · [bar] median, and the 5th-95th percentile' is crammed into one tiny mono line and reads as noise. The same explanation is better written in the footnote under the board and in 'Rounding'. Give it a small labelled diagram of one cell (big figure, full digits, bar and whisker, Runs) placed beside the category tabs.
6. Account for the 117 Series that are not on the board. 'Series in the API 187 / 70 on the board' appears in the hero and twice more, but nothing on the page says what the other 117 are (groups? other Methods? requests v1?). A reader who has been taught to trust exact counts will notice. One sentence near the board fixes it.
7. Choose the body face deliberately. The condensed display caps and the mono are characterful and well matched, but the running sans (hero paragraph, row descriptions, the 'Behind every figure' text) looks like a wide fallback system sans and makes those passages read generic. Choose a text face that sits with the other two, and tighten the hero paragraph to about 60 characters per line.
8. Shorten the phone page where the length is not earned. After the board, the five machine cards (phone-light-05/06) take almost two full tiles to repeat specs that fit a compact five-row table with the SKU and AWS quote expandable, and the 'Behind every figure' steps take another long stack. The board earns its length; the reference material does not.

KEEP. The yellow-and-black signage point of view, carried consistently from the header to the footer: condensed caps for row titles, numbered sections, colour-coded category tabs and left rules (MEM/CPU/OS/DSK/NET), and a dark mode that is a real counterpart, not an inversion. The board's structure: an ID per row, what is measured, the unit and direction, a plain-English description, 'One repetition:' stated exactly, then per machine the shortened figure, every digit, the per-row bar with p5-p95, and the Run count. The phone transposition into one card per benchmark with machines as rows is right. The disk caveat banner ('These rows measure the volume as much as the machine') is candid and exactly what an agent's user needs. The machine cards that quote AWS's own price string with the SKU and rate code. The For Agents section: four commented curl commands with copy buttons, a real JSON excerpt whose highlighted value is traced back to board row OS 08 c8i.2xlarge, a schema table, and the versioning promise. The Method quoted word for word with the percentile formula, and the Rounding note.

FALSE / MISLEADING. (a) A big flip clock reading '17:07 UTC' looks like the current time; the small 'NEWEST RUN STARTED' label is easy to miss, and the departure-board conceit encourages the misreading. (b) DSK 12 is described as 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes when 64 are kept submitted', which is a count or rate, but the figure is MEDIAN TIME in µs per completed read. Make the description match what is shown. (c) The JSON excerpt's Run (136.389 µs) and the Series median (136.370 µs) both display as '136.4 µs' in the caption, so it reads as though this Run is the median. Show one more digit, or say that they differ. Nothing else looked invented: the Run counts, dates, gp3 limits (about 131 MB/s, about 3,000 IOPS at QD64) and price strings agree with each other everywhere they appear.

v5.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Make the 14x5 grid comparable at a glance, not just readable (desktop-light-00 bottom to desktop-light-02 top). Every row is about 160 px tall, so the grid runs about three screens and the machine headers (m5.large ... c6i.8xlarge, with prices) scroll off after the first row; in desktop-light-01 and -02 you cannot tell which column is which without counting. Root cause: each cell stacks four lines (rounded figure, exact figure, p5/p95, counted Runs) and each row label stacks four levels of text. Fix the cause: (a) merge the rounded and exact figures into one line, with the leading significant digits in full weight and the trailing digits in a lighter tone, as the hero's 'Exact' line already does in red, so each figure appears once and stays exact; (b) put p5/p95 and the Run count on one small line; (c) move the 'One repetition: ...' sentence behind a disclosure or into the row's Series link. That should roughly halve the row height. Then make the machine header row sticky, or repeat it at each category rule (Memory/Compute/Operating system/Disk/Network).
2. Mark the best figure in each row. The direction is already stated ('Higher is faster' / 'Lower is faster'), but nothing shows which column wins, so every row means reading five 4-digit numbers. Bold the best cell, or put a thin in-cell bar on the same zero-based scale as the hero's 'The same benchmark on all five' chart. That chart is the most legible thing on the page, and the table drops its idea. On phone (phone-light-01 to -05) the same marker on the winning card would help just as much.
3. Show spread visually, not only as text. 'p5 908.5 · p95 1073.1' (Write 8 KiB durably, c8i.2xlarge) and 'p5 141.0 · p95 184.0' (mutex, c6i.8xlarge) are the interesting outliers, and they read the same as tight ones. A tiny p5-p50-p95 tick on each cell would make an unstable machine stand out.
4. Replace the two clock-time KPIs in section 02 (desktop-light-02: 'Newest Run 17:07', 'Oldest Run 23:36'). Huge time-of-day digits say little, and the oldest Run (10 Nov 23:36) sits oddly beside the hero's '11 November to 19 November' for its Series. Lead with the span and cadence ('9 days, 36 boots per machine'), with the exact timestamps as the small line, as they already are.
5. Disk rows: make the unit match the words, and name the limits. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' says 'How many direct reads ... completes' but shows µs per read. Add a bold derived line like the mutex row's '17.50 ns per critical section' only if the Derivation holds it; otherwise reword the description to 'time per completed read'. The disk note says these rows hit gp3's IOPS and throughput limits. Stating which limit each identical column shows (131.1 MB/s, 333.3 µs) would turn five identical numbers from 'is this broken?' into evidence.
6. Section 04 machines (desktop-light-03, phone-light-07): the raw AWS price-dimension paths ('/sources/0/terms/OnDemand/8D49XP...pricePerUnit/USD') wrap over two to four grey mono lines per machine and are the noisiest thing on the page. Keep the quoted AWS description, and make the path a single truncated link or a disclosure; the price file is already linked in the intro.
7. Phone code blocks: the JSON excerpts in 'From a figure to its evidence' (phone-light-06) are cut off at the right edge ('.../v1/series/a', '"evidence": "https://api.ledgermath.com/runs/202'). Either wrap them, or shorten the long values with an ellipsis so that the address you are teaching is visible. If they scroll sideways, show that they do.
8. Phone length is about 13,800 CSS px, nearly all of it the 70 cards. The card pattern (machine left, figure right, range under it) is properly designed for the width. Once change 1 shortens each card, consider collapsing each benchmark to its five main figures with the detail on tap, so the provenance and API sections are reachable without a long scroll.

KEEP.
- The first screen. 'AWS machines, measured four times a day.', the two-paragraph explanation, the copyable curl in the hero, and the 'Newest Run' / 'Boots every day, UTC' header together answer what, for whom and how fresh within seconds.
- The hero's exact line: the significant digits strong, the rest lighter, underlined and linked to its Series file. It is the best answer on the page to 'exact but readable'; spread it to the table (change 1).
- 'From a figure to its evidence, in two reads', with real JSON that matches the figures shown (p50 12502615200.030773 = 12.50 GB/s; the mutex Run's 136389 ns against 136.4 µs). That is exactly what an agent author needs, and it builds trust through consistency.
- The disk-section note explaining identical figures; the mutex row's per-critical-section line; the counted-Run count on every cell; 'Failed Runs are kept, never dropped'.
- The dark mode: the curl box inverts to a light block on black instead of vanishing, the red is lifted for contrast, and the bars invert cleanly.
- The restrained Swiss type system (one grotesk, mono only for addresses, one red accent), carried through consistently.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED.
- Section 02's 'Figure' card says 'Nothing rounded', while the large figures everywhere are rounded. The section 01 intro does say 'The large figure is rounded for display', but a skimmer meets the contradiction. Change 1 removes it at the source; otherwise reword the card to 'the published figure is exact; the large digits are a display rounding'.
- The red column highlight on m5.large carries over from the hero into the table. Because m5.large is the slowest in almost every row, red reads as 'worst/alert' rather than 'the figure featured above'. Consider a neutral highlight in the table, or drop it after the first row.
- Nothing else looks invented: the 14 benchmarks, 5 machines, counts and prices are consistent across the hero, the grid, section 02 and the JSON excerpts.

v6.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Say what the disk instruments are actually measuring. On desktop-light-01, '10 Read a file sequentially' shows ~131.1 MB/s on all five machines. That is 125 MiB/s, the gp3 volume's baseline throughput cap. '12 Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' shows 333.3 µs on all five, which is 1/3000 s, the gp3 baseline of 3,000 IOPS. Both charts are ZOOMED to six digits, so differences of 0.1% (131.09 vs 131.28) look like a ranking of machines. They are noise on top of a volume limit. Add one line to each card, e.g. 'All five sit at the root gp3 volume's 125 MiB/s cap', and drop the zoom, or keep it and mark the spread as within the cap. An agent reading these charts or the API will otherwise conclude something false. The cause is that a ZOOMED chart has no way to say 'these are equal'; build that state into the chart.
2. Fix the wording on card 12. 'The time until one direct read completes … with 64 kept submitted' reads as latency, but with 64 in flight the latency would be ~21 ms. The figure is time per completed read, i.e. inverse throughput. Say so in the subtitle and in the Every digit row label.
3. Thin out the Every digit table (desktop-light-02). 'p50 / p5 / p95 / n' is repeated in all five machine columns and 'Runs' 70 times, so the labels are a fifth of the ink. Put the row labels once at the left of each benchmark row, order them p5 · p50 · p95 (low to high, as the charts draw them), and drop the word 'Runs' to a column-head unit. The decimal alignment and the lighter trailing digits are excellent; keep them.
4. Account for 187 Series vs 70 figures. The strip (desktop-light-00, 'SERIES 187') and 'How a figure is made' both say 187, but the page shows 70. A careful reader will ask where the other 117 are and whether figures were chosen. Add one clause, e.g. '70 shown here: the default settings; the other 117 (other params/builds) are in series.json', linked.
5. Give agents a real handoff. 'Point an agent at the API' should go to a copyable prompt or an llms.txt-style block ('Start at /v1/index.json; every figure carries its Series file; cite it'). Right now it is a button with no visible promise. On phone (phone-light-08) the four curl lines are cut off at 'v1/inde…', 'v1/seri…', so the reader cannot see which file each fetches. Wrap them, or show only the path under a shared base URL.
6. Fix the phone header collision on card 08 (phone-light-03): 'Machinens per critical section · median, 4 digits' overprints 'Machine' onto the unit. Let the unit wrap below, or shorten it to 'ns / section'. On the same phone charts, '14.43' on card 02 sits off the right edge used by the other figures.
7. Cut the phone length. It is ~11 screens of 1,688 px. The instrument index grid (phone-light-01) is a good idea, but every card still carries a full Settings/One-repetition footer, the machines are five tall cards, and the Every digit table swipes one machine at a time, which defeats the comparison it exists for. On phone, transpose the table: one benchmark per block, five machines as rows, p50 with p5–p95 under it. Collapse the Settings footers behind the Every digit disclosure.
8. Merge the duplicated numbers and compress the Method section. 6,335 and 187 appear in the strip and again in 'How a figure is made'. The 'Method series v1, in the API's own words' block (desktop-light-04) and the 'requests v1' paragraph ('A Series is this Method's when any of its Runs' streams holds a request…') read as raw spec text. Keep the R type 7 formula and the 'counted' list, put the rest behind a disclosure, and rewrite the requests v1 paragraph in plain words. Also explain under the strip why the newest Run started at 17:07 when boots are at 16:10 (Runs follow the boot in sequence). Otherwise the schedule and the timestamp look inconsistent.

KEEP: The headline, which says what, how often and why to trust it in one sentence. The hero instrument with its annotated p5/median/p95 and the open 'every digit' panel: it teaches the chart grammar before the grid. One consistent dot-and-whisker grammar across all 14 cards, the same scale order (cheapest first) everywhere, explicit 'more/less is faster', units in every header, and an honest ZOOMED badge with a from-zero inset. Card 00, the price as the first instrument. The machine cards that quote the AWS price-file string verbatim with 'Where in the price file'. The dark API band with a real series.json excerpt tied back to the 19.58 at the top. The 'One Run, as its Series' file holds it' record, whose 136389 ns / 10,000 = 13.64 matches the mutex chart. The boot clock. Dark mode is carefully done, not inverted.

FALSE OR MISLEADING: The zoomed disk charts (items 1 and 2) imply machine differences that are really a gp3 volume limit, and card 12's subtitle describes latency where the figure is time per completion. Machine network specs mix 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit' as AWS writes them. That is faithful, but a normalised value next to each would stop misreadings. Nothing else read as invented; the counts (6,335 / 187 ≈ 34 Runs per Series, about 35 boots between 11-10 and 11-19) are internally consistent.

v7.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. The 14x5 grid is too tall and too far down. On desktop it starts at about y=1650 (desktop-light-00, bottom) and its 14 rows take about 2,900 px (desktop-light-01 to -02), because the left column (title, sentence, direction pill, unit sentence, setting line) makes every row 150-200 px tall while the figure cells use 40 px. The root cause is that the left column holds the whole benchmark description. Keep the name, the unit and the direction pill there, and move the sentence and the setting line to a smaller second line or a disclosure. Then the grid fits in about one and a half screens and can be compared at a glance. Also collapse the 'Every figure in the answer' ledger in the Q&A card by default on desktop, as the phone already does, so the grid starts near the second screen.
2. Align the figures. In desktop-light-01 the integer parts start at different x positions in the same column (12.50 at about x=424, 3.481 at 432, 571.42 at 417, 3296.71 at 409), and none of them lines up with the machine header above, which is left-aligned at x=408. Align on the decimal point with tabular figures, so magnitudes can be read down a column. Fade the trailing 10-12 digits a step further: bolding the first four significant digits is the right idea, but the grey tails are still loud enough to make every cell look the same width.
3. The 5th-95th percentile span is promised in the intro ('Under each figure, its median and its 5th to 95th percentile span') but you can hardly see it: a 1-2 px pink smear at the end of each bar, invisible on most rows (random memory, syscall, disk). Because every row is drawn from zero, a tight span cannot show at this bar length. Either draw the whisker clearly (a darker colour, end caps, a minimum visible width) or print the span as a number next to the Runs count (for example 'p5-p95 847.97-892.07' or '+/-2.6%'). It is the main honest signal of noise on the page, and right now it is decoration.
4. Mark the winner in each row. Each row says which way is faster, but to find the best machine you have to read all five long numbers. A small marker on the best cell, or a muted 'x1.00 / x3.84' ratio under each figure, would make the grid answer the question a reader actually brings to it.
5. The highlighted cell for the cited figure (Sort row, c8a.2xlarge, desktop-light-01) fills the whole row height, so a pink slab sits under empty space; in dark mode (desktop-dark-mid, top) it shows as a brown block hanging down beside the description text. Make the highlight hug the figure, the bar and the Runs line.
6. The hero's way in for agents ('GET v1/index.json / the way in, for agents', stats strip, right) is a relative path with no host and no copy button. The full https address and the copy buttons only appear about 3,500 px later, in 'Point your agent here'. Put the full URL on that tile with a Copy button, or move 'Point your agent here' above the grid; the nav already has 'For agents', so the order on the page should agree with it.
7. On the phone (phone-light-01 to -05) the grid becomes 70 stacked machine rows, with the machine name repeated 70 times. That is a real redesign, not a squeeze, and it reads well, but at roughly 13,000 CSS px the page needs a way to move around: a sticky or top jump list of the five groups (Memory, Compute, OS, Disk, Network), or a compact five-line block per benchmark with shorter names.
8. Small typography: the left-column unit sentences wrap badly ('ns per hash of the / same 64 bytes'; 'syscall(SYS_getpid), which enters the kernel / every time'), and the small grey monospace setting lines are close to the edge of legibility in light mode. 'The same numbers, for you' is bottom-aligned against a five-line paragraph, which leaves a large empty block above the heading.

WHAT IS STRONG AND MUST BE KEPT
- The worked question and answer as the hero's proof: a real question, the answer with its exact figures, footnote markers tied to the three GETs in order, and a ledger mapping each figure to its JSON field path. It is the clearest demonstration I have seen of 'an agent can cite this', and it makes the page distinctive.
- The agent's restraint line ('I haven't compared machines or worked out a cost per sort') is a good touch of honesty.
- Provenance throughout: Runs counted in every cell, AWS's own price wording quoted on each machine, the boot-time timeline, newest and oldest Run to the nanosecond, the counted/failed split, the Methods with their definition counts.
- The notes on the Disk and Network groups explaining why the five machines read alike (the gp3 volume, S3). They stop a reader drawing a false conclusion from identical numbers.
- The palette (warm paper, ink, one rust accent) and the serif, sans and monospace system, carried into a dark mode that holds up well.
- The phone's 2x2 stats grid, its collapsed Q&A panels and its machine cards.

ANYTHING FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- The Q&A is presented as a transcript ('A developer, to their agent' / 'The agent, after reading three files'). If it was not produced by a real agent run against the API, label it as an example; if it was, say so and date it. Either way it should not be ambiguous.
- The timeline puts the boots at 04:10, 10:10, 16:10 and 22:10, while the newest Run 'started 17:07:23' and the cited Series' newest Run 16:47. A boot followed by about an hour of runs is plausible, but nothing says so, and a reader may think the schedule is off. Label the dots 'boot' and add a line on how long a batch runs.
- '14 x 5 ... every digit' and 'requests v1, 13 definitions' are unexplained jargon on first read; 'requests v1' in particular is never introduced.
- The intro says 'Each figure links to its Series' file', but the cells show no link affordance (no underline, no icon). Either show it or drop the claim.

v8.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST

1. Make the headline table's bars say what they are and help a comparison (desktop-light-01/02, phone-light-03..06). The lede above the table says 'the bar under each is its 5th to 95th percentile', but each bar is really a track filled from zero to the median, scaled to the row's largest value, with a small p5–p95 whisker at its end. A reader who trusts the legend misreads every row. On top of that, a long bar means 'best' in the GB/s rows and 'worst' in the ns/µs rows, and nothing marks the winner. Fix the cause: state the encoding exactly ('bar: median against the row's largest; whisker: p5–p95'), and mark the best machine in each row with one quiet device (a bold figure or an accent tick), so the direction no longer depends on reading 'more is faster' / 'less is faster' in the label column. In the four Disk rows and the S3 row every bar sits pinned at the right end and carries no information. Consider a row scale that starts nearer the data, labelled as such, or drop the bar when the spread is under ~1% and say 'all within x%'.

2. Shorten the phone table by about 40% (phone-light-03..06). Each benchmark is a card with five two-line rows: machine name and number on one line, the bar alone on the next. That takes the table to roughly 6,000 CSS px and pushes 'Point your agent at the source' far down the page. Put the bar on the same line, to the right of the number, or under the number's light tail at half height. Also make the Memory/Compute/… chips sticky as a section index on phone, so the length has a way through it.

3. Show the table, not only one figure, before the fold on desktop (desktop-light-00). The hero card is excellent, but the page's main asset, 14×5 exact figures, starts about 3,000 px down, behind a stat strip and a five-step explainer. Move 'The headline table' up to sit directly under the hero, ahead of 'Why the numbers can be checked' and 'How it works', or put a three-row teaser of it at the bottom of the first screen. Developers who arrive to compare machines should not have to scroll past marketing to get there.

4. Rework the stat strip (desktop-light-00, middle band). '17:07 UTC, newest run' repeats the freshness line directly above it, and the 24-hour dial is too small to read (its '00'/'12' labels are ~8 px) and needs a legend to decode. Meanwhile '187 Series served' sits next to a table that shows 70, and the reconciliation ('Figures from 70 Series in a snapshot of 187; the others measure other settings and builds') is hidden in a footnote under the table. Either say '70 shown here of 187' in the strip, or swap that stat for one that carries more weight, such as the median count of Runs per figure (about 36).

5. Strip the internal vocabulary from the prose. Examples: 'disk_read_sequential's row' in the Disk note (the row is titled 'Read a file sequentially'); 'Counted: true, group A' in the Run example (desktop-light-03; 'group' is never explained); 'Derivation', 'R type 7'. Use the visible row titles, and explain 'group' in a word or drop it. Typeset the percentile formula in the Method section as a formula block, not as inline prose with floor brackets; at the moment it is the hardest-to-read paragraph on the page.

6. Add the open-source link (footer, nav). For a project whose whole pitch is 'check us', the only footer link is 'Font licences'. There is no repository link and no link to the benchmark source or how to add a benchmark. Put the repository in the nav next to 'Data API' and in the footer.

7. Bring the agent way in nearer the top and make it complete (desktop-light-02/03). The curl blocks with Copy buttons and the real series excerpt are very good. But the hero's 'Use the data API' is the only route to them, and the section sits after the full table. Add a one-line 'give your agent this' snippet (the index URL plus one sentence on what it holds) into or right under the hero. Say once, plainly, that the addresses are static JSON with no key and no rate limit (if true), and give the size of series.json so an agent knows whether to fetch it whole.

8. Small number details. In the Machines table, Network mixes 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit', and Storage reads '1 × 1875 NVMe SSD' with no unit. These are AWS's words, as the page says, but keep AWS's string as-is in a smaller second line and lead with a normalised value (Gbit/s, GB), so the row can be scanned. In the desktop table the figures sit left in their columns with ad-hoc padding (' 3.481' vs '14.428'); align each column on the decimal point, as the phone version already does.

STRONG, KEEP
- The hero card 'One figure, traced to its source' is the best idea on the page. It shows the exact median, the B/s value as stored, a correctly proportioned p5–p50–p95 strip, Runs counted and failed, the date span, the setting, the Method, the zone and price, and the Series file address. It shows trust where a claim would only assert it.
- The 'every digit, first four dark' treatment answers the project's no-rounding rule with readable figures, and the optional 'Round to four figures' toggle respects both readers.
- The figures agree with one another wherever they can be checked: 36 Runs over 11–19 Nov at four boots a day, the 136389.47 ns mutex Run ÷ 10,000 ≈ the c8i figure, 131.1 MB/s = the gp3 throughput cap, ~333 µs ≈ 3,000 IOPS, and 35+37+36+42+37 = 187. That rigour is the brand.
- 'One step further: a Run inside a Series file', with real Run and boot evidence URLs, and the Method definitions published as the API publishes them.
- Warm paper palette with one rust accent, a serif display face with mono for identifiers, and a dark mode that is a true counterpart, not an inversion. The five-step 'From a cold boot to a figure with a source' line drawing is clear and bespoke.
- Benchmark rows carry unit, direction and a one-line plain description of a repetition.

FALSE OR MISLEADING
- The legend 'the bar under each is its 5th to 95th percentile' does not describe the bars drawn (see 1). This is the one real misstatement.
- '187 Series served' next to a table of 70 figures reads as a contradiction until the footnote is found.
- Nothing else reads as invented. The page attributes the hardware specs and prices to AWS's price file, with its date and copy time.

ref:artificialanalysis.ai.notes: Intelligence, time and cost each get a chart with units or scoring direction, and the three distinct questions survive the move to stacked phone cards. Version notices and a dated changelog make revisions visible, though the angled model names are slow to match across charts and several later plots show only a legend and empty space in the captures.

ref:benchmark.clickhouse.com.notes: The title identifies the workload immediately, with methodology, reproduction and submission links close enough to inspect before accepting a ranking. The system filters consume the entire desktop first screen, and on the phone the ranked bars finally appear beneath a dense field of miniature orange labels.

The desktop hero offers agent setup, a sample company and a local option, while the phone directs a new reader to save the project for later and shrinks the product screenshot until its details are hard to read.

ref:instances.vantage.sh.notes: Region, billing period and precision sit directly above the instance rows, so a desktop reader can establish the basis of comparison at a glance. The MCP button and API announcement give developers two clear entry points, but on the phone that announcement covers rows in a viewport barely wide enough for the instance name.

ref:planetscale.com.notes: The latency chart has a percentile legend, a migration caption and a link to the benchmarks, giving the performance claim a concrete place to investigate. The opening customer grid delays that evidence by dozens of logos, especially on the phone where it wraps into two columns.

The latency panel names its workload, distinguishes warm and cold reads and links the benchmark, though the large difference between those readings is carried by very small labels.

v1.notes:
Changes, in priority order

1. Give phone readers a complete route through the book. In phone-light-00 the chapter strip cuts off at IV, and the desktop link to “How agents read it” disappears beside the curl command. Wrap the five chapter links onto two lines and restore a developer-guide jump by Copy. Someone coming for disk latency or the JSON schema could then skip several screens of memory and CPU results.
2. Make the worked entry do double duty on phone-light-00. Attach the three explanations to the first actual sequential-read result, with the longer key expandable. The current example spends much of the first screen teaching a number that appears again immediately below. Showing two machines sooner would teach the comparison as well as the notation.
3. In the ledger cells (desktop-light-00 and desktop-dark-mid), give the percentile bounds and the trailing median digits a little more size and contrast. The bold leading digits scan beautifully, but resolving close values such as the five sequential disk rates requires reading the smallest type. Preserve the full decimal strings and keep the run links visually separate from the bounds.
4. In the phone masthead, put us-east-2 alongside the freshness line. Desktop gives that scope before the ledger; on phone even the first machine price appears without a visible region. It is a material qualifier for using either time or cost in an estimate.
5. In the annotated JSON specimen (desktop-light-01, phone-light-05), move field explanations outside the code area or put them behind a single annotation toggle. The italic prose between properties makes the payload harder to scan and leaves the scope of Copy ambiguous.

Keep

The masthead answers what gets measured, how often and for whom in three lines. The repeated machine names and prices at desktop chapter boundaries make the lower rows usable in isolation. Keep the common-scale rules, direction beside each unit, per-cell counted Runs and nearby disk and S3 caveats. The latter explain why nearly identical results across machines matter. The dated price source, annotated real Run and exact totals carry the book-of-record idea all the way to the footer.

Potentially misleading

The mobile example shows 12.502… without the GB/s visible in its desktop counterpart. Put the unit on the example wherever the number stands alone. The other claims read consistently across the screenshots.

v2.notes:
Changes, in priority order

1. On phone-light-00, put the first five-machine comparison directly below the freshness summary and jump links. Keep the index command handy there and group the other commands under the API link. Someone landing here to choose a machine can currently reach the bottom of the first screen without seeing a single measured value.
2. In the disk and network rows (desktop-light-01, phone-light-03), give overlapping ranges a group label such as “All five p5–p95 ranges overlap.” Keep the exact best median marked, but give the group observation equal prominence. For random 4 KiB reads the bright star attracts the eye to a few hundredths of a microsecond while four quiet approximation signs carry the more consequential information.
3. Give the data categories a compact jump menu accessible throughout the phone tables (phone-light-01 through -03). The first category index works on the way in. A reader at mutex who wants to compare machines on hash or find the API again faces a long scroll back.
4. In desktop-dark-mid and phone-dark-mid, brighten the percentile ranges, counted-run labels and trailing median digits slightly. Preserve the heavier leading digits. The secondary lines are where a reader checks whether a difference is worth acting on, and they recede especially far against the dark ground.
5. In FILES (desktop-light-02, phone-light-05), show the mutex sample's exact per-critical-section result alongside the raw repetition time and divisor. Identify it as one Run. This would complete the worked example and let a developer check their interpretation of the API against the unit in DATA.

Keep the manual-page structure, warm paper and restrained ink colours, and the immediate, copyable index command. The stable ordering of machine types, bold leading digits, per-cell range and sample count, and repeated desktop column headings make a difficult grid usable. The phone version gives each machine a labelled row. Keep the unusually specific disk explanation about the root gp3 volume, the date on the prices, and the distinction between kept and counted Runs.

Potentially misleading wording: FILES says “Every figure in DATA links one” immediately after describing the per-Series file. The earlier DATA introduction more precisely promises that each median links to its Series. Use that wording consistently so readers know which numbers lead to evidence. I saw no apparent invented claims.

v3.notes:
Changes, in priority order
1. Bring the first five-machine comparison up on phone-light-00. The abstract repeats the headline's scope, then a machine roster, four timestamps/counts, a fourteen-item index and a dense caption precede row a. Lead with the worked measurement and its 36 Runs, retain the copyable API entry, and fold the benchmark index and schedule details behind clearly named controls. That would let a reader compare machines much sooner.
2. Give the exact tails and Run counts in Table 1 a larger minimum type size and stronger contrast, especially on desktop-light-00 and desktop-dark-top. The bold leading digits already win attention by weight. Use the spare outer width for the matrix if needed. In the sequential disk row the machines are close enough that the quieter digits matter.
3. Put a drawn key immediately above Table 1 showing a median tick, a p5–p95 band and a counted-Run label on one sample line. The caption currently makes the reader decode all three in prose. On phone-light-02 several ranges disappear into their ticks, so demonstrate the narrow-range case too.
4. Replace 'chosen by a written rule' in the Table 1 caption with the selection criterion or a direct, named link to it. Table S1 calls these the 70 headline Series, while the API lists 187. A reader checking a price/performance comparison needs to know why these particular Series represent each machine.
5. In the API section on phone-light-04, put the single-Series command and its annotated response together. The command, prices command and long listing caption currently intervene in the path from requesting one measurement to recognizing it in JSON. The API quotation repeats the introductory prose and could yield that space.

Keep the publication-like hierarchy, warm paper and ink palette, restrained red annotations and the five-column desktop matrix. The mobile benchmark groups genuinely recompose the comparison around one operation. The shared zero baseline within each benchmark, unit and direction beside its name, hourly price in the desktop machine heading and explicit root-volume qualifier all help readers interpret a result. Keep the trace from the opening memory example to its Series ID, exact JSON field, unit conversion and counted Runs. The compact supplementary table and collapsed mobile appendix give specialists access to all percentile digits.

Potentially misleading: 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 submitted' followed by 'One completed read' on phone-light-02/03 leaves room to read the figure as the latency experienced by an individual request at queue depth 64. v4.notes:
Changes, in priority order
1. Put one real five-machine comparison on the first phone screen. In phone-light-00 the latest time, introduction, command and second status panel consume the viewport. Keep the dated timestamp and command up top, fold the schedule and lifetime totals under a details control, and move the cell key beside the first result. Let readers see what they can actually query.
2. Give the five category jumps a compact sticky home on phone. By phone-light-03 the reader is several screens from the chooser, with the entire disk section still ahead. Include the current category and spell out the destinations in the chooser.
3. Give each median a visible link treatment. On desktop-light-00 the board introduction promises a Series file behind each figure, but the numbers look like ordinary bold table text. A consistent underline on the median alone would make the evidence discoverable without adding 70 labels.
4. Increase the size and contrast of the exact values, percentile bounds and Run counts, especially in desktop-dark-mid. They carry the evidence but get the smallest type. Reclaim space by placing the unit in the row heading and giving the exact figure its own full-width line on phone.
5. Put a short scale explanation at the first chart, in the reading key on desktop-light-00 and phone-light-00. Say that the five machines share a scale within each benchmark and that the capped segment spans p5–p95. The fuller explanation arrives after NET 14, too late to guide the first comparison.

Keep the yellow masthead, split-flap timestamp and condensed headings. They make the instrument recognizable in both themes. The stable machine order, direction labels and printed ranges make comparisons possible even without the colors. Keep the disk caveat immediately above the disk rows. The OS 08 example in phone-light-06 is especially good: it follows one highlighted Run value through unit conversion, distinguishes it from the Series median, and supplies the evidence address.

Potentially misleading: the JSON panel on desktop-light-02 calls itself an excerpt ‘as it is’, yet samples are elided with an ellipsis. Label it ‘excerpt with samples omitted’ so someone working from the example knows exactly what was edited.

v5.notes:
Changes, in priority order

1. Give the percentile endpoints enough precision to distinguish them when they differ. In the buffered disk-read row on phone-light-03/04, several intervals read “p5 131.1 · p95 131.1” and their whiskers occupy about a pixel. Keep the zero-based bars for comparing machines, and make the full endpoints available alongside the exact median in the row detail. This would let a reader investigate the near tie the graphic actually shows.
2. On desktop-light-01 and desktop-dark-mid, enlarge the trailing digits and percentile/count line a little. The leading digits do their job beautifully, but checking a particular figure requires reading the smallest type in the densest part of the page. Use the generous vertical space within each row to give that text room.
3. On phone-light-00, keep the schedule in the masthead and shorten the introduction to the machine count, region, workload and purpose. The four UTC times appear twice before the first figure. Reclaiming those lines would bring the exact value and its comparison closer to the headline.
4. Beside the mutex example on phone-light-06 and desktop-light-03, show the unit conversion on one line, from the JSON p50 in ns to the displayed number in µs. Then label the final evidence URL as the file to fetch next. This would make the example reproducible even for someone skimming the code blocks.

Keep the single red example threaded from headline-size result through the exact linked number, five-machine chart and highlighted first table cell. The phone comparison genuinely works vertically, with machine names, medians, sample counts and range bars visible together. Keep the benchmark index, category return links, visible freshness, copyable entry command and distinction between the 70 displayed Series and 187 published. The warm paper, heavy rules and restrained colour hold up in dark mode too.

Potentially misleading wording: “From a figure to its evidence, in two reads” gets the reader to the evidence address in the second response. Reading the evidence file itself takes another request. The illustrated records make the distinction clear on close inspection.

v6.notes:
Changes, in priority order

1. On phone-light-05 through -08, make the second pass through all 14 benchmarks an explicitly opened “Compare all 70 exact medians” view. Each instrument already offers “Every digit”. Keep the all-figures view directly addressable from the benchmark chooser. Each cell right-aligns the whole string, bold head plus tail, so the tails' different lengths push the bold heads around (compare 12.502 and 3.481 in the m5.large column, or 3 296.712 and 571.429). 3. Say which machine is best in each row. The bars mean opposite things from row to row: on ↑ rows the longest bar is best, on ↓ rows it is worst. A newcomer scanning for the winner has to read the arrow every time. Add a quiet mark on the best median in each row (a dot, an underline or a heavier tick), and perhaps flip ↓ rows so that a short bar always reads as good. Rows j-l are almost identical on all five machines because they measure the gp3 root volume's limits: 131.0 MB/s is 125 MiB/s, and 333.3 µs per read with 64 in flight is 3,000 IOPS. Footnote b hints at this through a phrase nobody has met ('the headline rule's words'). Move the bar legend out of the Table 1 caption into a small visual key above the table (a drawn bar with labels for median, 5-95 and n), cut the caption to one line, and keep the exactness argument in §4.3 alone. 1. The digits you compare do not line up. Every cell right-aligns the whole string, strong digits plus a light tail of varying length, so the bold part drifts sideways from cell to cell. Desktop-light-01, Hash row: 571.42 starts about 200 px left of where 76.68 starts. Phone-light-01, Read memory in random order: 3.481 and 14.428 begin at different x, so you cannot read down the column. Give the light tail a fixed-width slot and align the strong digits on the decimal point. This is the main thing holding `numbers` back.
2. Strong digits are truncated while p5/p95 are rounded, so some cells show a p5 above the median. Desktop-light-01 and phone-light-03/04, Read a file sequentially, m5.large: figure 131.2|84…, then 'p5 131.3 · p95 131.3'. It reads as an error. Use one rule for both, either round the percentiles the same way or show them to the same precision as the strong digits, and check every cell for p5 > p50 or p50 > p95 as displayed.
3. Every light tail is underlined as a link. Across 70 cells that is a wall of grey hairlines, and the light digits are already low-contrast grey on cream (worse in dark, desktop-dark-mid). Put the link on the whole cell, or underline only on hover or focus, and lift the tail's contrast a step. The exactness will read as intended rather than as noise.
4. The bars encode raw magnitude, so on 'Lower is faster' rows the longest bar is the worst machine. On 'Higher is faster' rows it is the best. Nothing in the bar marks good or bad. Either mark the best cell per row (weight or a small marker), or state the direction next to the bar. As it stands, the eye reads 'long = good' and gets the Compute/OS/Disk rows backwards (e.g. Hash 571.42 on m5.large).
5. Phone: the JSON walkthrough (phone-light-06/07) wraps long URLs mid-token ('…c2d748916b1 / 9.json', run and boot URLs). The curl blocks also break 'curl' and its address onto two lines, with the prices URL split mid-date. Let code blocks scroll sideways (or shorten the JSON with …), and keep each curl on one scrollable line. On a page about exact addresses, broken addresses are the wrong detail to get wrong.
6. Phone length: the table is about five 844 px screens of stacked rows (phone-light-01 to 05). The per-benchmark stack (machine, figure, p5/p95, Runs, bar) is well designed, but 70 tall rows is a lot. Tighten each machine row to one line plus the bar, and drop the repeated '· N Runs' when it is the same within a benchmark. That alone cuts it by roughly a third.
7. Section headings 02 and 03 (desktop-light-02) are poster-sized and run to three lines ('For agents, and the developers who run them'), with large dead bands beside and below them. They compete with the hero number for the top of the hierarchy. Bring them down a size so the hero figure stays the one huge thing on the page.
8. Explain or drop 'Series 187 · 70 of them in the table' (desktop-light-02). A reader is left wondering what the other 117 are. Also explain why the hero is m5.large's read-memory figure, the second-lowest of five ('the first figure of the table below' explains where it comes from, not why). Either say in a line what the other Series are, or choose a hero that makes a point, e.g. the spread across the five on the side chart.

WHAT IS STRONG AND MUST BE KEPT.
The first screen does the job in seconds: a plain headline ('AWS machines, measured four times a day.'), freshness and the boot schedule in the header strip, the curl to index.json with Copy, then one figure set huge with its exact value printed beside it. That 'large for display, full beside it' device is this design's idea, and it states the no-rounding policy without saying it. The What/Where/From/Source strip under the hero is excellent provenance. The desktop table is honest and rich: the header carries vCPU, GiB and price, 'cheapest first'; each row has unit, direction and a one-line description; each cell has p5–p95 and counted Runs; the mutex row adds per-critical-section time. The Disk note explaining that gp3 caps all five machines at the same numbers is exactly the honesty this project needs. 'Where every figure comes from' (big counts, 0 failed, Run → Series → Method → Figure) and the two-read walkthrough from a table cell to its evidence JSON are the best agent/developer onboarding I have seen in this set. The Swiss typographic discipline (one red, cream ground, numbered sections, hairline rules) is carried consistently through light and dark.

ANYTHING FALSE OR MISLEADING.
Nothing looks invented. The figures agree across the page: e.g. the mutex walkthrough's p50 136370.579… ns matches the table's 136.37… µs. Two things read as wrong: the p5-above-median display in Read a file sequentially (truncation against rounding, item 2), and the bars implying 'longer is better' on time rows (item 4).

v6.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Rewrite the lower half of 'How a figure is made' (desktop-light-04, phone-light-11/12) for a newcomer, not for someone who has read the repo. Phrases such as 'A second example, from another Series: the one file the snapshot keeps whole' (set in bold mono, which makes it worse), 'The group its split facts put it in', 'scripts/check-events.py', 'blob_url_template with {hex} replaced', 'not a --quick stream' and 'requests v1 ... takes the same Series as series' are internal vocabulary. 2. Explain why the Run counts differ. The stats strip says '6,335 counted, 0 failed', yet the counts run from 36 (m5.large) down to 32–33 (c8i, and the S3 rows), and a careful reader will ask where the missing Runs went if none failed. Add one line, in the stats strip or the legend, that says what makes a Run absent rather than failed (a boot that never came up, no capacity, and so on). Without it the '0 failed' reads as too clean.
3. Remove the empty space in the instrument grid (desktop-light-01, -02). Each chart is pushed down to line up with a row-mate that has a VOLUME LIMIT box and a ZOOMED strip, which leaves about 180 px of blank space above the charts in 09 Echo, 11 Read 8 KiB and 13 Write durably, and in the top of 12/14. Move the VOLUME LIMIT note under the chart, next to Settings, and keep only the one-line ZOOMED strip above it. Or let the cards stop aligning their charts. The grid would then read as a dense instrument panel, not a table with holes.
4. The hero chart (01 Read memory sequentially) appears again unchanged as the second card of the grid, about one screen later on desktop and on phone. Keep the hero, since it teaches the marks, but make the grid's 01 card visibly 'the one above' (collapsed, or 'shown at the top' with a link), or put a different benchmark in the hero. That saves a screen on phone.
5. Phone 'Every digit' (phone-light-05 to -08) repeats all 70 figures as 14 more cards, right after 14 charts that each already open to every digit. Collapse this section on phone to a jump list or a single disclosure. It is the main reason the phone page runs about 13 screens. On those cards the p5/p95 lines are also not aligned on the decimal point, although the medians are.
6. Fix the 08 Lock and unlock a mutex header (desktop-light-01, phone-light-03). 'ns per critical section · median, 4 digits' wraps onto two lines, so the unit row sits higher than every other card's. Shorten it to 'ns / critical section' or let the unit wrap under 'Machine'.
7. In the dark API section (desktop-light-03/-04), '"Version 1 only ever gains fields."' sits alone as an unattributed pull-quote. State it as a plain fact next to the schema links ('v1 only adds fields; nothing is renamed or removed'). The SETTINGS/RUNS/PERCENTILES/EVIDENCE 2×2 then trails below the left column while the JSON panel ends, which leaves the section lopsided. Fold the 2×2 into the JSON panel's annotations or place it above the prompt.
8. Contrast of small grey text: the Settings/One repetition labels, the card subtitles, and the lighter digit tails in the Every digit table are small grey text on cream, near the limit for comfortable reading, especially in the 12 px Settings rows. Darken the secondary grey one step in light mode. The tail digits can stay lighter, but they need to be legible.

KEEP. The hero tells you what this is, who it is for and why to trust it inside the first screen: the plain headline, the agent sentence, the curl, and a real instrument with its every-digit panel. The dot-and-whisker charts with the exact figure and the Run count on every row, all on one scale with the cheapest machine first. The ZOOMED treatment: the from-zero minimap with the box and the axis-break mark is honest and clever. The VOLUME LIMIT callouts, which say the row measures the volume, not the machine. Setting the digits past the fourth significant one lighter, so 'exact' stays readable. The internal consistency: the JSON p50 19581876183.050716 B/s is exactly the hero's 19.581876183050716 GB/s, and the mutex Run's 136389 ns per 10,000 sections gives the table's 13.64 ns. The machines cards quoting AWS's own price string with 'Where in the price file'. The boot clock. The phone's 01–14 jump grid and the '↑ All benchmarks' links, which are real phone design. The dark mode is carried through properly, including the warm every-digit panel.

FALSE OR MISLEADING. Nothing invented that I could find, and the dots I checked are drawn at the right values. The one risk is the 17-significant-digit tails: they are float64 representation digits, not measured precision, and calling them 'exact' without saying so could mislead a reader into thinking the instrument resolves to 1e-15. One clause in the Every digit intro would fix this ('as stored; digits past the fourth are not significant'). Also see item 2: '0 failed' next to unequal Run counts needs an explanation to stay credible.

v7.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. The phone answer cell is broken (phone-light-02, bottom: Sort 1 MiB, c8a.2xlarge row). The heavy '858' wraps onto its own line at the top right of the pink box, and '.4353094482422' sits on the line below beside 'c8a.2xlarge · THE ANSWER'. This is the one cell the whole page builds towards, so it has to be the best-set figure on the page. Put the 'THE ANSWER' tag on its own line, or under the name, so the median keeps the same column as the other four rows, and never let the figure break inside itself (keep it all in one nowrap span).
2. The p5-p95 ranges are rounded to about four digits everywhere in the table (desktop-light-01/02, every phone row), while the page says 'every digit' and 'Nothing is rounded'. The rounding also produces a visible falsehood: in 'Read a file sequentially', the m5.large median is 131.2840… but its range prints as '131.3-131.3', so the median looks like it falls below its own 5th percentile. The cause is shortening the ranges. Either print them the way the medians are printed (four heavy digits, then the rest light), or label them openly as shortened, with the full digits a hover or tap away. Then check that no median ever prints outside its range.
3. The 14×5 grid, which is the product, begins about 1,600 px down on desktop (desktop-light-00, bottom), two screens below the fold, after the whole worked answer. Keep the worked answer, since it is the thesis, but give it less height. Collapse the 'Every figure in the answer, and where its file holds it' table on desktop the same way the phone already does. Make the hero's '14 × 5' tile a link to the grid. Then the first screen and a half show both the story and the grid.
4. Comparing across a row is harder than it needs to be. A bar measures magnitude, not goodness, so in a 'lower is faster' row the longest bar is the worst, and in a 'higher is faster' row the longest bar is the best. The reader has to re-read the direction chip on every row. Add a quiet marker to the best median in each row (the direction is a fact, so this is not a judgement), or draw the bars so that 'better' always reads the same way. The bars stay honest either way, but they become useful at a glance.
5. The light tail digits of the medians, and the 'p5-p95' and 'N Runs' lines, are small grey mono on cream (desktop-light-01, all cells). At 1440 px they are close to unreadable. The heavy and light contrast is a good idea, but darken the tail one step and raise the cell's secondary line by about 1 px, in light mode especially. Dark mode handles this better.
6. In the machines section (desktop-light-02 bottom, 03 top; phone-light-06), the network column mixes 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit'. If these are AWS's own strings, say so in the column header ('as AWS words it'), or add a normalised Gbit/s beside them. As it stands it looks like careless data entry. The AWS price sentence quoted under every price is good provenance, but it can be smaller and lighter, since it repeats five times.
7. Phone length: the table runs to roughly seven phone screens' worth of tiles. The section chips (Memory, Compute, OS, Disk, Network; phone-light-01) are the right idea. Make them stick while the reader is inside the table, so the length is navigable rather than just long. Consider collapsing each benchmark after its first, say, three rows, or showing the five machines as one tight row per benchmark.
8. Small details: the italic agent caveat ('I haven't compared machines…') is honest, but it reads as an odd, apologetic voice at the end of the showcase answer. Shorten it to one clause. The Disk and Network notes (the left-ruled callouts) are excellent, so keep them.

STRONG, KEEP
- The thesis: one real question answered from three named GETs, every figure traced to file and field (including the raw '"0.4310800000"' price string and the ns-to-µs conversion stated outright), and the same cell then marked in the grid and in the machines list ('PRICED IN THE ANSWER ABOVE'). This is the most convincing provenance device I have seen on a page of this kind, and it explains the agent use case without a word of marketing.
- The disclosure 'The exchange is written for this page; every figure in it is read from the API's files'. It is honest and pre-empts doubt.
- The hero: a clear headline, a plain-language subhead, a stat strip, and the index.json GET with Copy, all above the fold on both desktop and phone.
- Every cell in the grid carries its own Run count and a link to the Series file. The four-heavy-digits-then-tail treatment respects 'every digit' while staying scannable. The direction chip and the unit sit on every benchmark, and the c8a column header is tinted throughout.
- The 'Point your agent here' block: three curl commands, a paste-ready prompt, and the schemas listed by name.
- The provenance section: the boot timeline with the newest Run placed on it, oldest and newest Run to the nanosecond, runs and failures, and the versioned Methods.
- A consistent palette (cream and rust, warm near-black in dark mode, with a salmon accent that holds up), and a serif display face with sans and mono that carries a point of view all the way down. The phone page is designed, not squeezed: there are per-benchmark cards, collapsible GET and field lists, and a 2×2 stat grid.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- 'Nothing is rounded' and 'every digit', while the ranges in the grid are rounded. This produces the m5.large 'Read a file sequentially' case, where the median prints outside its own p5-p95 range (131.284 against 131.3-131.3). Nothing else read as invented: the times, the counts, the boot schedule and the price-copy timestamp agree with one another across sections.

The same Run (01a1cb79…) is walked through three times: in the hero card's beige 'ONE OF ITS 33 RUNS' box (desktop-light-00, right), in the JSON excerpt, and again in the 'ONE STEP FURTHER' table under it (desktop-light-02, right). Show it once. Take the beige box out of the hero card and let the API section's Run table be the one place that goes a level down. That fixes the next two problems as well.

KEEP. The big-digits-then-small-remainder treatment of exact figures (13.63 then 7057904052734), carried into the table as dark first four significant figures and grey trailing digits. It answers 'exact but scannable' better than anything else I have seen for this brief. Keep decimal alignment within each column, the unit under each benchmark name, the per-section machine header repeated at each group, and the 'Round to four figures' toggle (off by default). Keep the three-up proof strip (6,335 Runs / the four boot times on a 24-hour axis / 70 of 187 Series). Keep the API section's labelled curl boxes, each with a one-line 'what you get', plus the schemas line. The type system works and is consistent: serif display, sans body, mono for identifiers and figures. So does the cream, rust and ink palette, and the inverted dark API band in light mode. FALSE / MISLEADING. I found nothing invented. The hero's p5/p50/p95 match the JSON excerpt ÷ 10,000, the Run's figure ÷ 10,000 matches its stated per-section value, and the disk rows that are equal across machines are explained by the gp3 note. Two places could mislead. (a) The hero strip's unlabelled zoomed axis, next to a table that promises zero-based bars (see 8). (b) 'Measured four times a day… boots at 04:10, 10:10, 16:10, 22:10' next to 'newest Run 17:07'. That is consistent, but without a word saying a boot's Runs take about an hour, a reader may think a timestamp is wrong.

ref:benchmark.clickhouse.com.notes: An honest benchmark page. Methodology, 'Reproduce and Validate the Results', a JSON benchmark and Add a System are the first links you see, and each result row carries its own date, category tag and a relative multiplier (×1.62) in an aligned column. ref:helix-db.com.notes: A distinct, consistent identity: a dotted pixel display face, mono body text, warm paper colours, corner-bracket buttons. The way in for agents and developers is the primary action ('Set up with your agent', a copyable 'run it locally'). Provenance is shown, not claimed: '60 of 62' match bars, sources named for each field, an example answer with footnoted citations and monthly counts. The mono body text on a long line is slow to read, and the beige-on-beige panels are low in contrast. The phone page is designed: it says honestly that the product needs a bigger screen and offers a GitHub star instead.

ref:instances.vantage.sh.notes: The densest, most directly useful figure table of the set: exact CoreMark scores, monospaced API names, filters on every column, region and price-unit controls right where you need them. ref:planetscale.com.notes: A strong, consistent point of view: all-monospace prose, hairline-ruled logo grid, ASCII-style diagrams, dotted section rules. ref:turbopuffer.com.notes: The best of the set at turning figures into the pitch. A plain claim ('search every byte'), a small architecture diagram, a scale line (1T+ documents, 10M+ writes/s), then a working cost calculator and p50/p90/p99 bars for warm and cold namespaces, with the workload stated and the benchmark repo linked, plus a limits table that gives 'seen in prod' next to each limit. The dark-to-light bands, pixel-shadowed boxes and mono type are carried through with care. On phone it reflows well, though the limits table wraps awkwardly. A developer has no command or snippet on the home page.

ref:vercel.com.notes: Excellent type and restraint (the tight grotesk headline, the generous whitespace), but 'Agentic Infrastructure' with a triangle says little to a newcomer in ten seconds, and the page has almost no figures besides a customer stat. In this headless capture everything below the first section is blank (scroll-triggered content never appeared), so most of the page's length was empty: in practice it is a polished template with not enough said.

Machines, On-Demand card (desktop-light-00 top-left; phone-light-00 after card 01): the grey bar sits right after the GiB column, so it reads as memory, but it is drawn from price (i4i and c6i are both 64 GiB yet the c6i bar is twice as long). Caption the object as one entry from the series list and put the conversion directly below it with its unit, ns per critical section. This keeps the connection to the headline figure while giving developers an unambiguous JSON example.

Put ‘for agents’ in the eyebrow and use the space to bring the comparisons up. On phone the first exact figure just fits the first screen while its unit falls below it.

ref:artificialanalysis.ai.notes: A clear claim, 'Independent analysis of AI', in a confident serif, with the three headline metrics (intelligence, time, cost per task) shown as labelled, value-on-bar charts on the first screen. A dated changelog signals freshness. The rotated model labels are hard to read, especially on phone; the many provider hues make comparison harder rather than easier; and the way in for a developer or an agent isn't on the home page. In this capture most charts further down are blank (they load lazily), which leaves long empty boxes.

ref:benchmark.clickhouse.com.notes: An honest benchmark page. Methodology, 'Reproduce and Validate the Results', a JSON benchmark and Add a System are the first links you see, and each result row carries its own date, category tag and a relative multiplier (×1.62) in an aligned column. Its main fault is that the filter wall of hundreds of beige chips takes the whole first screen on desktop, and nearly two screens on phone, before any result shows. The type and colour are default-browser utilitarian, with little hierarchy beyond the H1.

ref:helix-db.com.notes: A distinct, consistent identity: a dotted pixel display face, mono body text, warm paper colours, corner-bracket buttons. The way in for agents and developers is the primary action ('Set up with your agent', a copyable 'run it locally'). Provenance is shown, not claimed: '60 of 62' match bars, sources named for each field, an example answer with footnoted citations and monthly counts. The mono body text on a long line is slow to read, and the beige-on-beige panels are low in contrast. The phone page is designed: it says honestly that the product needs a bigger screen and offers a GitHub star instead.

ref:instances.vantage.sh.notes: The densest, most directly useful figure table of the set: exact CoreMark scores, monospaced API names, filters on every column, region and price-unit controls right where you need them. It costs a lot: numbers are left-aligned and don't share a precision (95,158.796 next to 192,539.11), the 'Updated' line is hidden under a cookie banner and a promo pop-up covers the table, and nothing says where a score comes from or how many runs are behind it. The phone page is the desktop table cut off at the right edge, which is not a design.

ref:planetscale.com.notes: A strong, consistent point of view: all-monospace prose, hairline-ruled logo grid, ASCII-style diagrams, dotted section rules. It reads like engineers wrote it, and the p50/p95/p99 before-and-after graph links on to a benchmarking page. But the first screen is a wall of mono paragraphs with no single big claim, the logo grid takes several screens (worse on phone, where it runs to two columns of dozens of cells), and there are few figures for a page that sells speed.

ref:turbopuffer.com.notes: The best of the set at turning figures into the pitch. A plain claim ('search every byte'), a small architecture diagram, a scale line (1T+ documents, 10M+ writes/s), then a working cost calculator and p50/p90/p99 bars for warm and cold namespaces, with the workload stated and the benchmark repo linked, plus a limits table that gives 'seen in prod' next to each limit. The dark-to-light bands, pixel-shadowed boxes and mono type are carried through with care. On phone it reflows well, though the limits table wraps awkwardly. A developer has no command or snippet on the home page.

ref:vercel.com.notes: Excellent type and restraint (the tight grotesk headline, the generous whitespace), but 'Agentic Infrastructure' with a triangle says little to a newcomer in ten seconds, and the page has almost no figures besides a customer stat. In this headless capture everything below the first section is blank (scroll-triggered content never appeared), so most of the page's length was empty: in practice it is a polished template with not enough said.

KEEP: the ledger as the first thing under a two-line hero, with five rows of figures above the fold on desktop. The decimal-aligned figures with bold leading digits and lighter grouped tail digits: this is the best answer yet to 'exact but scannable'. The unit column with a ↑/↓ direction arrow instead of 'higher is better' prose. The per-row bars from zero. The roman-numeral sections and the double red rule. v2.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Desktop table (desktop-light-00, ~y 470 to 1640): the machine header row scrolls away long before DISK and NETWORK, so by mid-page the five columns are unnamed. Make the header row sticky. First cut it to three short lines per column (name, '8 vCPU 16 GiB', '$/h'), with the CPU on one line in a short form ('Xeon 8175', 'EPYC 9R45', 'Xeon 8375C'). Today it is five lines, and 'Intel Xeon Platinum / 8175' and '(Granite Rapids)' wrap.
2. Evidence per figure is one click too far. The only path from a number to its Runs is the FILES list at the very bottom, plus a URL template the reader has to fill in. Link each benchmark name (or the row itself) straight to its /v1/series/<id>.json. That brings provenance and the API into every row without adding a word.
3. How many Runs stand behind a figure is hidden behind '[+] exact p5, p95, counted runs', which sits alone at the far right of the legend row (desktop ~x 1040, y 428), where it is easy to miss. If the count is short, show it on the row's unit line ('GB/s ↑ · 452 runs'). Either way, move the toggle next to the legend so it reads as part of the key.
4. Remove the dotted underline under every bold leading part. That is 70 decorations that suggest a hover, and a phone has no hover. Bold against grey already marks the leading digits.
5. Choose one metaphor. The man-page frame (NAME / SYNOPSIS / STATUS / DATA / FILES, LEDGERMATH(5)) is the idea. The markdown '## MEMORY' prefixes and the '[+]' fight it. Drop the '##'. LEDGERMATH(5) also appears three times (both top corners and the footer); keep the man-page header and footer, but the top-right copy could carry the latest-Run time instead.
6. Phone (phone-light-02): the machine key (vCPU, GiB, CPU, $/h) comes after all 14 benchmarks, so a phone reader meets 'c8i.2xlarge' 70 times before learning what it is. Move it to sit just after the DATA nav, as five one-line rows, and delete the bottom MACHINES section. That moves content without adding any.
7. Make units unambiguous with fewer words. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 submitted · μs' does not say whether this is per read or per batch; 333 μs is about 1/3000 s, the gp3 IOPS ceiling, so the unit should say 'μs per read'. 'methods  series v1 requests v1' is opaque to a newcomer: separate the two links with ' · ' at least, so they do not run together as one phrase.
8. Contrast of the range marks: in light mode the 0→p5 track and the p5–p95 band are close in tone, and most bands come out as a 2 px tick. Darken the band one step so the spread reads where it exists (as on the c8i rows and the mutex rows). Leave the scale honest.

KEEP. The economy: the whole desktop page is about two screens, with almost no prose, and every word earns its place. The man-page conceit is carried through desktop, phone and dark mode consistently, and it fits a tool for developers and agents. The decimal-aligned, exact figures, with bold leading digits and grey tail digits, keep the exactness and still let the eye compare at a glance. The p5–p50–p95 range is built into each cell. The curl command with copy is in the first screen, and the STATUS block puts freshness, schedule, the price date, the Run count, the region/AZ and the methods all in view. The 'root EBS gp3 volume' note on DISK is the right kind of caption: short and necessary. The phone page is a real re-layout (benchmark → five machine rows → bar), not a squeezed table. The dark theme in amber on near-black is good.

FALSE OR MISLEADING? 'runs 6,335 since 2026-11-10, 0 failed' does not square with the page's own '14 benchmarks × 5 machine types, four times a day'. That is 280 a day, about 2,700 to 2,800 since 2026-11-10. Either 'Run' means something other than one benchmark on one boot, or the figure is wrong; make sure the two statements agree. The prices and CPUs shown match what I know of us-east-2 On-Demand and these instance families, and Read a file sequentially at about 131 MB/s matches the gp3 baseline, which lends credibility.

v3.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Strip the parts of the paper costume that carry no information (desktop-light-00 and phone-light-00/02). Remove 'Data report' next to the logo, the 'ABSTRACT' and 'DATA AVAILABILITY' small-caps labels, the section numbers '1'/'2'/'A', the 'Table 1.'/'Table 2.'/'Table S1.'/'Listing 1.' prefixes, and the 'Supplement' heading. Make the footer's 'Method SERIES v1' plain. The journal look already comes through in the serif, the rules and the caption style, so the labels are furniture on top of it. Each one is a word to read, and together they make the page feel more written than it is.
2. Get rid of Table 2 (Machines) by folding it into Table 1's column headers. Those headers already give the machine name, vCPU, GiB and $/h. Add the processor as one short line ('Xeon 8175', 'Granite Rapids', 'EPYC 9R45', 'Ice Lake'), and add storage only for i4i ('1×1875 GB NVMe'). That cuts a whole section that repeats the five names and five prices a second time on desktop and on phone, and it shortens the phone page by about a screen.
3. Show how many Runs stand behind each figure in the table itself. Right now the count is behind the 'Range and Run count per figure' link and the collapsed Table S1, so the main table never shows per-figure n. If n is the same down a machine's column, put it once in that column's header ('n 91'). If not, add it as a small figure in the same grey as the trailing digits. The band is the only red on the page, so the eye goes straight to the noisiest cells (c6i mutex, c8i TCP, c8i 'Unpack 8-bit') and reads them as warnings. Pick one left edge for the text and let only the table body break out, or left-align the title with the table so the first screen has one axis.
