7. Tone the trailing digits down a step further on desktop: lighter colour, and a little more space before the next column's bar. The bold head carries the figure well. The 12-digit tails ('615 200 030 773') make each cell's right edge ragged and push into the gap between columns.
8. Dark mode (desktop-dark-top, phone-dark-*): the bar tracks and the small grey tails lose contrast against the warm black. Raise both slightly; the rest of the dark theme is well judged.

KEEP: The journal-report point of view, carried through in type, rules, the reference list and the footer. It is the most distinctive thing here and it suits a project that publishes evidence. The title says exactly what the project is, with figures. The single provenance line (first Run, latest Run, prices copied, '6,335 counted, 0 failed'). The curl command with copy, right in the first screen. The References block, which lists the API's files with schema links: a better way in for an agent than prose. Exact figures shown as a bold head plus smaller grouped trailing digits, decimal-aligned, with thin-space thousands ('3 296.712'). That keeps the exactness without wrecking scanning. Units and the higher/lower arrow tucked under each benchmark name. Per-benchmark scales from zero, which keeps the disk rows honestly flat. The phone layout pivoted to one block per benchmark with the five machines as rows: a real phone design, and its length is earned by the 70 figures. Table 1's figures visible within the first desktop screen.

FALSE OR MISLEADING: 'All 187 Series' in References [2], beside a page that shows 70 figures, leaves a reader asking where the other 117 are. Either say in two words what they are or drop the count. 'Runs 6,335 counted' implies there are Runs that were not counted. If any exist, the uncounted number belongs next to 'counted' and 'failed'. If none do, 'counted' is a word that raises a question. Trailing-digit lengths vary from 3 to 13 digits between cells with nothing to say why ('22.854 877' against '12.502 615 200 030 773'). That may read as different precision, so the table's caption should make it clear with as few words as possible.

v4.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST.
1. The exact digits break up the figures. In every cell the value appears as a bold '12.502' followed by small grey groups '615 200 030 773' with spaces between them (desktop-light-00, all board cells). That looks like several numbers, not one. On the phone (phone-light-00/01) the groups wrap onto two more lines under each value, so each cell reads as a stack of three numbers. This is the main thing between the board and great. Keep every digit, but make the tail read as part of one number: the same baseline, no wrapping, hair spaces or no spaces rather than word spaces, and a lighter tone that is still clearly attached. On the phone, show the tail on one line, clipped or fading at the column edge, with the full figure on tap. As it is, the uneven tail lengths ('877', '016 25', '409 797 986 016 3') also make the columns ragged.
2. Remove the machine-name row repeated at the top of every category band (MEMORY, COMPUTE, OS, DISK, NETWORK: 'm5.large n=36  c8i.2xlarge n=33 …'). On desktop the dark column header already names the machines, so this is five rows of noise. Show n once, in the column header, when it is the same for the whole column, and mark only the cells that differ (the per-cell 'n=35'/'n=33' in the c6i.8xlarge memory rows already does this). On the phone, a sticky machine header would do this job better than repeating the names five times.
3. The header says 'RUNS 6,335', but the n values on the board add up to about 2,400, and the agents block says 'all 187 Series' while the board shows 70 cells. A careful reader will try to reconcile these and fail. Make the header count match what the board shows, or label it in two or three words, e.g. '6,335 runs · 187 series'. Don't add an explanation.
4. The flip-clock '17:07 UTC' is the biggest element in the top-right card (desktop-light-00) and takes most of the phone's first screen (phone-light-00), but the time of the newest run is the least useful fact in the card. Make the clock smaller, and give the space to the round slots plus runs, failed and region. The progress bar and green dot under '16:10' also suggest that round is still running; say plainly whether it is.
5. The 14 benchmark names are set in all-caps condensed display type ('READ MEMORY IN RANDOM ORDER', 'RANDOM 4 KIB READS, 64 SUBMITTED'). This is slower to read than sentence case, and several names wrap to two lines, which makes row heights uneven. Keep the display face for section titles, and set the row names in sentence case or a narrower size so each fits on one line.
6. FOR AGENTS (desktop-light-01): the right column holds two disclosure rows with vague labels ('ONE RUN, IN ITS SERIES FILE', 'WHERE EACH PRICE IS READ') above a lot of empty space. Either give them labels that say what you get, or drop them and let the API documentation link carry that. The curl block is good; don't make it longer.
7. From a figure on the board there is no visible route to its evidence or its series file; the dotted underline under each median hints at one but doesn't say. One small, consistent affordance, such as the series id on hover/tap or the underline linking to the series JSON, would make provenance concrete without adding text.
8. Dark mode: the grey tail digits and the 'n=' labels lose contrast on the near-black cells (desktop-dark-mid), and the pink CPU band is louder than the other categories. Even the category tints out.

KEEP. The hero is the best of its kind I've seen for this brief: one headline, one sentence and one curl command, and in ten seconds you know what this is and that it's for agents. The yellow-and-black identity is carried consistently through the nav, the price chips, the highlights, the footer and dark mode. The range bar (0 to row max, p5–p95 band, median tick) with its one-line legend shows the spread without words. The unit and direction chip on each benchmark ('GB/s ↑', 'µs ↓') is economical. The note 'root EBS gp3 volume on all five' under DISK explains why the disk rows are flat, in six words. Prices sit with each machine in the column header. The phone board is a real redesign (one card per benchmark with five columns), not a squeezed table. The FOR AGENTS curl list with copy buttons and schema links is the right way in.

FALSE OR MISLEADING. Nothing reads as invented, but the 6,335 / 187-series header does not visibly match the n values on the board (see 3). The progress bar under '16:10' implies a round in progress that the page doesn't otherwise confirm. The nanosecond 'As of 2026-11-19 17:07:23.182448102 UTC' in the footer is precision for show; harmless, but it's not a figure anyone uses.

v5.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Hero figure (desktop-light-00, desktop-dark-top, phone-light-00 top): the tail digits '2615200030773' sit on their own line under 'GB/s', in the same red, so they read as a second, separate 13-digit number, not as the rest of 12.50. Use the convention the table already uses: the tail runs straight on from '12.50' on the same baseline, smaller and lighter, with the unit after it (or above it). The hero should teach the head/tail reading that the table relies on, not contradict it.

On desktop, compare 'Read 8 KiB from disk' (582.9) with 'Random 4 KiB reads' (333.3), and the whole GET 4 KiB from S3 row (22.92 is about 60 px right of every other head). Then the heads form a clean column you can scan, and the tails still show every digit.

At about 33 to 36 Runs per Series across 70 Series, a reader gets roughly 2,400, not 6,335. If 6,335 counts something else (repetitions, every attempt, all benchmarks over all time), the label must say which in a word. As it stands it looks like an error.

The figures match only after dividing by a repetition count the page never shows, so someone cross-checking sees two different numbers. Pick a Series whose JSON field is the figure the table shows (a GB/s or µs row), so the sample checks against the table at a glance with no note.
5. Disk section: all five machines read 131.x MB/s and 333.x µs. That includes i4i.2xlarge, whose header implies local NVMe. A reader can't tell what storage was measured. Name it in two or three words on the Disk section label (for example 'Disk · <volume type>') rather than in a caption. Don't add prose.
6. Close the empty band between the provenance strip and '01 The figures' (desktop-light-00, about 870 to 1000 px; the same gap on phone). Pulling the section up by around 100 px brings the machine header row onto the first desktop screen, so the first screen shows that a whole grid follows, not just one featured figure.
7. Number of Runs per figure: only the hero says 'of 36 Runs'. One small count per column header, or per row next to the unit, would carry provenance into the grid without clutter. Then drop the repeated machine-name header rows above Compute, OS, Disk and Network, and use one sticky header row instead.
8. A link to the source repository in the header nav, next to Figures and API. The project is open source and invites new benchmarks, and the footer is an empty black band carrying only the wordmark.

KEEP. The headline 'AWS machines, measured four times a day.' with one short line of context and the curl command with Copy beside it: a newcomer knows what this is and how to use it within seconds. The provenance strip (boot times, date range, Runs kept, Methods, price date) is terse and exactly right. The head/tail digit treatment gives every digit while staying readable. The 0-to-p50 bars with p5 to p95 whiskers, the machines ordered cheapest first with exact prices, and the per-row unit with '↑/↓ faster' are all good. The red rule over the m5.large cell in the table (and the red left mark on phone) ties the hero to the grid. The phone transposition (one block per benchmark, machines as rows, bars between name and figure) is properly designed, not squeezed. The API section is economical: base URL, three files with a few words each, schemas, the evidence URL pattern, docs. The heavy grotesk with a single red accent carries a clear point of view in both light and dark, and dark mode is well tuned (coral red, not pure red).

FALSE OR MISLEADING. (a) The hero tail on its own line reads as a separate number (point 1). (b) 'Runs kept 6,335' doesn't square with 33 to 36 Runs per Series (point 3). (c) The JSON sample's p50 doesn't visibly match the table figure for the same Series (point 4). Nothing else reads as invented; the identical disk figures look like a real platform limit, but the page gives no way to tell (point 5).

v6.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first.
1. Show how many Runs stand behind each figure, as a number rather than prose. The cards (desktop-light-00, all 14) show a median and a p5-p95 whisker but never n. The only Run count is the global '6,335 Runs kept' in the strip, and 'Runs' is hidden inside the collapsed 'Exact figures' disclosure. One token per card would do it, set in the unit corner already there (e.g. 'GB/s · 33'), and it shouldn't cost a line.
2. Make the Run counts reconcile. The strip says 6,335 Runs kept. The API sample (desktop-light-00 bottom, phone-light-02) shows a Series with "count": 33, and its p50 matches the c8i.2xlarge figure on card 01 (19.58 GB/s). 6,335 across 70 Series is about 90 each, not 33. A reader who checks will distrust both. Either make the sample representative or say what the 6,335 counts with a sharper label (e.g. 'Runs kept, all Series'), not with a sentence.
3. Make the zoomed-axis inset self-evident and consistent. Cards 10, 12 and 14 carry a second 0-to-N line beneath the axis. On 10 and 12 it marks the window with a red tick, but on 14 it marks it with a shaded box. Use the shaded window on all three, and start the inset with the same '//' glyph the legend defines, so the eye ties the inset to the break without any caption. In dark mode (desktop-dark-top) the axis ticks and grey whiskers sink into the background, and the whisker on card 08 i4i/c6i is the only range that reads well. These labels carry the units and the direction of 'better', so they need to read at a glance.

ref:artificialanalysis.ai.notes: A clear claim, 'Independent analysis of AI', in a confident serif, with the three headline metrics (intelligence, time, cost per task) shown as labelled, value-on-bar charts on the first screen. A dated changelog signals freshness. The rotated model labels are hard to read, especially on phone; the many provider hues make comparison harder rather than easier; and the way in for a developer or an agent isn't on the home page. In this capture most charts further down are blank (they load lazily), which leaves long empty boxes.

ref:benchmark.clickhouse.com.notes: An honest benchmark page. Methodology, 'Reproduce and Validate the Results', a JSON benchmark and Add a System are the first links you see, and each result row carries its own date, category tag and a relative multiplier (×1.62) in an aligned column. Its main fault is that the filter wall of hundreds of beige chips takes the whole first screen on desktop, and nearly two screens on phone, before any result shows. The type and colour are default-browser utilitarian, with little hierarchy beyond the H1.

ref:helix-db.com.notes: A distinct, consistent identity: a dotted pixel display face, mono body text, warm paper colours, corner-bracket buttons. The way in for agents and developers is the primary action ('Set up with your agent', a copyable 'run it locally'). Provenance is shown, not claimed: '60 of 62' match bars, sources named for each field, an example answer with footnoted citations and monthly counts. The mono body text on a long line is slow to read, and the beige-on-beige panels are low in contrast. The phone page is designed: it says honestly that the product needs a bigger screen and offers a GitHub star instead.

ref:instances.vantage.sh.notes: The densest, most directly useful figure table of the set: exact CoreMark scores, monospaced API names, filters on every column, region and price-unit controls right where you need them. It costs a lot: numbers are left-aligned and don't share a precision (95,158.796 next to 192,539.11), the 'Updated' line is hidden under a cookie banner and a promo pop-up covers the table, and nothing says where a score comes from or how many runs are behind it. The phone page is the desktop table cut off at the right edge, which is not a design.

ref:planetscale.com.notes: A strong, consistent point of view: all-monospace prose, hairline-ruled logo grid, ASCII-style diagrams, dotted section rules. It reads like engineers wrote it, and the p50/p95/p99 before-and-after graph links on to a benchmarking page. But the first screen is a wall of mono paragraphs with no single big claim, the logo grid takes several screens (worse on phone, where it runs to two columns of dozens of cells), and there are few figures for a page that sells speed.

ref:turbopuffer.com.notes: The best of the set at turning figures into the pitch. A plain claim ('search every byte'), a small architecture diagram, a scale line (1T+ documents, 10M+ writes/s), then a working cost calculator and p50/p90/p99 bars for warm and cold namespaces, with the workload stated and the benchmark repo linked, plus a limits table that gives 'seen in prod' next to each limit. The dark-to-light bands, pixel-shadowed boxes and mono type are carried through with care. On phone it reflows well, though the limits table wraps awkwardly. A developer has no command or snippet on the home page.

ref:vercel.com.notes: Excellent type and restraint (the tight grotesk headline, the generous whitespace), but 'Agentic Infrastructure' with a triangle says little to a newcomer in ten seconds, and the page has almost no figures besides a customer stat. In this headless capture everything below the first section is blank (scroll-triggered content never appeared), so most of the page's length was empty: in practice it is a polished template with not enough said.
